AGENCY:
Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Extension of approval of an information collection; comment request.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this notice announces the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service's intention to request an extension of approval of an information collection associated with the regulations governing importation of cattle and bison, specifically with regard to classification of regions at designated status levels for bovine tuberculosis and brucellosis, and establishing conditions for the importation of cattle and bison from regions with the various classifications.
DATES:
We will consider all comments that we receive on or before December 15, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by either of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
www.regulations.gov.
Enter APHIS-2026-1486 in the Search field. Select the Documents tab, then select the Comment button in the list of documents.
Postal Mail/Commercial Delivery:
Send your comment to Docket No. APHIS-2026-1486, Regulatory Analysis and Development, PPD, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Avenue, #AP760, Beltsville, MD 20705.
Supporting documents and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at
www.regulations.gov
or in our reading room, which is located in Room 1620 of the USDA South Building, 14th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC. Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 799-7039 before coming.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information on the regulations for bovine tuberculosis and brucellosis regionalization and associated importation of cattle and bison, contact Dr. Amber Kerk, Assistant Director, Regionalization Evaluation Services, Strategy and Policy, VS, APHIS, 920 Main Campus Drive, Suite 200, Raleigh, NC 27606;
AskRegionalization@usda.gov.
For more information on the information collection reporting process, contact Ms. Sheniqua Harris, APHIS' Paperwork Reduction Act Coordinator, at (301) 851-2538;
APHIS.PRA@usda.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Brucellosis and Bovine Tuberculosis: Importation of Cattle and Bison.
OMB Control Number:
0579-0442.
( printed page 65719)
Type of Request:
Extension of approval of an information collection.
Abstract:
Under the Animal Health Protection Act (7 U.S.C. 8301et seq.) the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of the U.S. Department of Agriculture is authorized, among other things, to prohibit or restrict the importation and interstate movement of animals and animal products to prevent the introduction into and dissemination within the United States of livestock diseases and pests. To carry out this mission, APHIS regulates the importation of animals and animal products into the United States. APHIS' Veterinary Services is the program responsible for regulating these importations.
The regulations in 9 CFR part 93 contain, among other things, provisions that address the risk that imported bovines (cattle or bison) may introduce or disseminate brucellosis or bovine tuberculosis (TB) within the United States. In 2020, APHIS amended its import regulations to establish a system to classify foreign regions at designated status levels for bovine TB and brucellosis; to establish provisions for modifying the TB or brucellosis classification of a foreign region; and establishing conditions for the importation of cattle and bison from regions with the various classifications.
TB is a contagious disease of both animals and humans. Bovine TB, caused by
Mycobacterum bovis,
can be transmitted from livestock to humans and other animals. Brucellosis is an infectious disease of animals and humans caused by the bacteria of the genus
Brucella.
The disease is characterized by abortions and impaired fertility in its principal animal hosts. Different
Brucella
species are associated with disease in different host species;
Brucella abortus
is associated with the disease in cattle and bison. There is no economically feasible treatment for brucellosis in livestock.
The activities include the request for regional classification and additional information about a region, an application for recognition of regional classification (TB and brucellosis), maintaining classification and reclassification, and the official identification and certification.
We are asking the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to approve our use of these information collection activities, as described, for an additional 3 years.
The purpose of this notice is to solicit comments from the public (as well as affected agencies) concerning our information collection. These comments will help us:
(1) Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(2) Evaluate the accuracy of our estimate of the burden of the collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(3) Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
(4) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, through use, as appropriate, of automated, electronic, mechanical, and other collection technologies;
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses.
Estimate of burden:
The public burden for this collection of information is estimated to average 14.6 hours per response.
Respondents:
Foreign animal health officials; importers and exporters.
Estimated annual number of respondents:
21.
Estimated annual number of responses per respondent:
3.
Estimated annual number of responses:
62.
Estimated total annual burden on respondents:
907 hours. (Due to averaging, the total annual burden hours may not equal the product of the annual number of responses multiplied by the reporting burden per response.)
All responses to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will also become a matter of public record.
Done in Washington, DC, this 30th day of September 2026.
Kelly Moore,
Administrator, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

articles.title: China unveils draft export controls on AI technologies and chips - Financial Times
articles.summary: China unveils draft export controls on AI technologies and chips  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the Artificial intelligence myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
China has proposed new export controls on technologies used in areas including AI models and agents and chip design.
The draft controls issued on Friday highlight Beijing’s growing focus on maintaining the security of rapidly developing domestic AI technologies amid intensifying rivalry with the US.
The export of leading AI models trained on sensitive Chinese data, as well as advanced AI agents used in areas such as critical digital infrastructure, defence and government services, would be restricted under the draft rules released jointly by the ministries of commerce and information technology.
The proposed expansion of China’s lists of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export, which the FT reported in July, would give Beijing greater oversight of transfers of advanced AI technologies overseas.
The move is partly aimed at closing what Beijing sees as a regulatory loophole exposed by US tech group Meta’s $2bn acquisition of AI app Manus, a deal Chinese authorities subsequently ordered to be unwound.
The draft controls issued on Friday also cover technologies used to design advanced processing and memory chips, packaging and networking equipment.
The proposed restrictions on the export of such technologies do not necessarily mean that products built using them will also be controlled. They would mainly prevent Chinese companies from transferring the underlying technology overseas, for example via acquisitions by foreign entities.
The draft rules also include several exemptions. Open-weight AI models — which can be run and customised by users — would be exempt if they were made publicly available and had not been trained on sensitive data.
However, the rules would allow restriction on the transfer of technology used in such open-weight models — potentially blocking the transfer offshore of ownership or key employees — if they surpassed 2tn parameters or were ranked top among global peers by performance.
The number of parameters refers to the size of an AI model’s neural network, with a higher count generally leading to greater capabilities.
Chinese AI start-up Moonshot’s latest K3 model, which caused a global stir this year as its performance approached top-tier offerings from Anthropic, has 2.8tn parameters.
Simpler approval procedures would also apply to Chinese companies building and operating AI data centres overseas, manufacturing their own chip designs abroad, conducting research with foreign partners or helping set international standards. Chinese tech groups ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent are expanding their overseas data centre capacity as restrictions imposed by the US and its allies limit their access to advanced chips in China.
The commerce ministry said in a statement the proposed controls would ban access to AI models trained on sensitive “core data”, but would not affect indirect access to other Chinese AI models from overseas, for example through apps or websites.
“The key distinction is whether restricted technology is being transferred from China to another country,” the ministry said.
China’s most recent revision to its export restriction list in 2025 added several lithium-ion battery manufacturing technologies to it, building on existing controls on strategically important sectors such as rare earth extraction and processing.
The latest proposed controls also cover some biomedical and solar technologies.
“It is crucial to ensure the safety and controllability of AI technology,” the commerce ministry said, adding that the curbs were intended to “prevent the misuse of AI technologies”.
“These technologies could pose risks to national and global security if obtained by malicious actors, and the restrictions are intended to prevent abuse and keep AI under human control,” it said.

AGENCY:
Office of Refugee Resettlement, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Request for public comments.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) is requesting a three-year extension with revisions of the Unaccompanied Refugee Minors (URM) Program ORR-3 Report and ORR-4 Report (Office of Management and Budget #0970-0034, expiration 11/30/2026). Revisions were made to reduce burden and streamline information collection.
Description:
The ORR-3 Report is submitted to report a youth's initial placement in the URM Program, termination from the program, or re-entry into the program. The ORR-3 is also submitted to report changes to the youth's case (
e.g.,
change in legal responsibility, change in foster home placement, etc.). The ORR-4 Report is submitted annually and at termination to report on the youth's receipt of services and outcomes. Proposed revisions to the forms include replacing multiple follow-up outcome reports with a single termination outcome report, replacing self-reported outcome measures from youth with provider-reported measures, eliminating select sub-types of ORR-3 reports, replacing or streamlining unclear questions and response options, removing unnecessary questions, and streamlining supplemental report instructions to integrate more guidance directly into the forms.
Respondents:
URM state/replacement designee agencies and URM provider agencies.
Annual Burden Estimates
The edits described above will result in a reduction in annual burden estimates of approximately 41 percent once implemented. Additionally, youth have been removed as a respondent to the ORR-4 Report; youth outcome measures will no longer be self-reported, instead providers will report youth outcomes. Revisions will be implemented after a 12-month implementation timeframe; the following burden estimates are specific to the revised versions following the 12-month implementation period.
( printed page 65749)

articles.title: US: Steel prices rise to highest level in over 4 years due to tariff impact. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: US: Steel prices rise to highest level in over 4 years due to tariff impact.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
This boosts profits for domestic steel producers, but at the same time drives up production and construction costs, increasing inflationary pressure on the world's largest economy .
 According to Fastmarkets, the price of hot-rolled steel coils, a widely used type of steel and a benchmark for pricing in the US market, has increased by 52% over the past year, reaching $1,255 per short ton (approximately 907 kg). This is the highest price since May 2022.
 The surge in steel prices reflects the mixed effects of the Trump administration's protectionist trade policies. While American steel mills benefit from higher prices and reduced foreign competition, manufacturing, construction, and data center development companies face increasingly high raw material costs.
 This development also poses a challenge for the Republican Party ahead of the midterm congressional elections on November 3rd, when inflation and the cost of living continue to be issues of particular concern to American voters.
 Josh Spoores, a steel research expert at CRU Group (a data and analytics firm), noted that import restrictions and the ever-changing US trade policy toward key partners like Canada and Mexico have led many businesses to limit their steel orders from overseas, creating a supply shortage.
 Despite being a net importer of steel, the US has seen a significant decline in steel imports this year. According to the American Iron and Steel Institute (AISI), imports of finished steel in the first nine months of 2026 decreased by 14% year-on-year, to approximately 13 million tons. Consequently, the market share of imported steel in the US market fell from 19% to 16%.
 Domestic supply is projected to continue facing pressure in the final months of the year, as many domestic steel mills undergo scheduled maintenance. According to Fastmarkets, the expected output impact between September and December is over 1 million tons.
 Richard Bourke, a senior analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, believes that US steel prices could continue to rise in the near future. Besides limited supply, the price of scrap iron – a key raw material in steel production – is also increasing earlier than usual at the end of the year.
 Mr. Bourke stated that negotiations for steel supply contracts for 2027 between producers and customers "so far have been favorable to steel producers, and discounts are likely to be lower than in recent years."
 Rising steel prices have significantly benefited major U.S. steel producers such as Nucor, Cleveland-Cliffs, and Steel Dynamics. Shares of Nucor – a leading steel producer – have risen more than 50% this year.
 Analysts predict that the revenue and profits of steel companies will continue to increase when they announce their third-quarter business results in the coming weeks.
 However, the long-term supply outlook could change as the U.S. pushes for the construction of more large-scale steel production facilities. Last month, President Trump announced plans to develop the $15 billion Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Iowa, with an expected capacity of 10 million tons per year and production scheduled to begin around the end of this decade. This news caused the stocks of some steel companies to fall due to concerns about increased future supply.
 Meanwhile, the gap between US steel prices and international markets continues to widen. Hot-rolled coil steel prices in the US are now about two-thirds higher than in Europe and nearly three times higher than in China . This is a significant difference that could undermine the cost competitiveness of US industries that rely heavily on steel.
 In China, steel exports remained near record levels, exceeding 10 million tons for the fifth consecutive month, despite concerns from trading partners about overcapacity and price competition.
 President Trump's policy of imposing a 50% tariff on imported steel is also causing trade tensions with Canada, one of America's important steel suppliers.
 Last month, Cleveland-Cliffs – one of the largest steel producers in the U.S. – announced an indefinite suspension of some operations at its Canadian subsidiary Stelco, potentially affecting around 500 workers.
 This decision exacerbates disagreements with the Canadian government , which has threatened legal action against Cleveland-Cliffs regarding its job retention commitments when it acquired Stelco for CAD 3.4 billion (approximately USD 2.4 billion) in 2024.
 Analysts believe the sharp rise in steel prices is demonstrating the double-edged effects of the tariffs pursued by the Trump administration. While protectionist measures have helped support the domestic steel industry, the increased raw material costs risk undermining the competitiveness of steel-producing industries, driving up prices and adding to inflationary pressure.
 With continued restrictions on imported steel supply and high demand for raw materials from various industries, the US steel market is projected to continue facing upward price pressure in the final months of 2026.

articles.title: As Tariffs Push Manufacturers to Reshore, Woods Distribution Offers Integrated 3PL Support for U.S. Producers - Newswire.com
articles.summary: As Tariffs Push Manufacturers to Reshore, Woods Distribution Offers Integrated 3PL Support for U.S. Producers  Newswire.com
articles.full_text:
Fort Worth logistics provider aligns warehousing, transportation, and packaging services with its mission to help re-industrialize America
FORT WORTH, Texas, October 16, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Woods Distribution, a Fort Worth-based third-party logistics (3PL) provider, is offering integrated logistics support to U.S. manufacturers that are reevaluating sourcing, production, and distribution strategies in response to an evolving tariff environment and renewed interest in domestic manufacturing.
Trade policy has been a moving target for manufacturers. According to Taylor's Q3 2026 Material Matters report, Section 301 tariffs on goods from China were upheld, keeping cost pressure on companies that depend on Chinese imports. For many producers, that uncertainty is accelerating conversations about bringing more production, assembly, and inventory closer to U.S. customers.
Reshoring, however, creates its own logistics challenges. Domestic production often requires new inbound flows of raw materials and components, additional storage near plants, and outbound distribution networks built for different volumes and destinations. Woods' approach, captured in its "Re-industrialize America" theme, is to give manufacturers a single partner that can support that shift from end to end.
"American manufacturers are making long-term decisions in a short-term policy environment, and they need logistics partners who can move with them," said Will Scherer, Director of Sales of Woods Distribution. "Our goal is to take warehousing, transportation, and packaging off their plate so they can focus on what they do best, which is building products here at home."
For industrial and manufacturing customers, Woods provides plant support services that coordinate inbound raw materials and outbound finished goods, along with shared and dedicated warehousing that can handle bulk and oversized pallets. Contract packaging and kitting teams work inside Woods' warehouses, allowing manufacturers to assemble kits, apply labels, and prepare retail-ready configurations without adding transportation legs.
On the transportation side, Woods operates its own trucks for local full truckload, less-than-truckload, box truck, and drayage service in Dallas-Fort Worth, while its in-house brokerage team handles nationwide FTL, LTL, intermodal, cross-border, and specialized freight. Cross-border capabilities are particularly relevant for manufacturers adjusting North American supply chains as sourcing patterns change.
Those capabilities are backed by Woods' relationship with Union Industrial Co., the Dallas-based private investment firm that Woods joined in April 2025. Together, warehousing, transportation, and packaging give manufacturers a single partner to coordinate inbound materials, storage, value-added work, and outbound distribution as their domestic footprint grows.
Manufacturers exploring these options can learn how Woods Distribution supports industrial supply chains with integrated warehousing, transportation, and packaging solutions.
"Reshoring is not a single decision, it is a series of operational changes that have to work together," Scherer added. "When one partner can store your materials, move your freight, and package your product, those changes happen faster and with a lot less risk."
With approximately 30 million cubic feet of warehouse space in Texas and 8 million cubic feet in Illinois, Woods supports manufacturers and brands in industrials, food and beverage, consumer packaged goods, retail, health and beauty, and apparel and footwear.
About Woods Distribution
Woods Distribution is a full-service third-party logistics provider delivering integrated warehousing, contract packaging, and transportation solutions across the United States. Built on disciplined execution and operational consistency, Woods supports manufacturers, retailers, and distributors with scalable logistics infrastructure designed to reduce complexity and improve supply chain performance. Learn more at https://woodsdist.com.

articles.title: Trump's tariffs are changing the global trade ecosystem - Al Majalla
articles.summary: Trump's tariffs are changing the global trade ecosystem  Al Majalla
articles.full_text:
American tariffs have gone beyond their traditional role of raising import costs and protecting domestic industries. As their scope widens and their terms change week-to-week, companies are reconsidering where they source goods, organise supply chains, establish production facilities, and seek alternative markets. So far, the main effect has been a redistribution of trade among markets, manufacturing centres, and commercial routes, with little evidence of a wholesale contraction in global commerce.
Trade data from the US, Canada, Europe, Asia, and the Gulf reveal a changing pattern of US imports, a reassessment of trade relations between Washington and its traditional allies, and the growing importance of economies capable of offering alternative manufacturing bases, transport routes, and markets. One of the clearest indications of the changing geography of American trade lies in the origins of its imports.
An analysis by the McKinsey Global Institute from January to May 2026, compared with the same period a year earlier, found that China’s share of total US imports had fallen by 2.7 percentage points, but the share of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) rose by 4.6 percentage points, and that of the rest of the Asia-Pacific region rose by 3.7 percentage points. Europe’s share declined by 8.1 percentage points, largely reflecting the waning effects of a surge in advance imports during 2025, particularly of chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and gold. The decline also extended to other categories, including cars.
These figures require careful interpretation. The shift in American imports cannot be explained simply as a transfer of trade from China to elsewhere. McKinsey says a product’s country of origin might not reveal where its value was created. Some Asian economies have become intermediate links in production chains that continue to draw on Chinese components and materials alongside inputs from elsewhere.
Broader trend
The broader trend is nevertheless clear: the US is diversifying its sources of imports without necessarily bringing manufacturing back to American soil. More recent US figures also suggest that tariffs have yet to produce a sustained decline in imports. In August 2026, American goods imports rose by 5.5% to $336.1bn, pushing the goods trade deficit up by 11.5% to $132.6bn. Goods continue to enter the American market despite higher tariffs, although rising import values are not the same as an increase in the actual volume of goods purchased.
Tariffs appear to be changing the routes and composition of trade more readily than reducing its overall flow. As a result, ASEAN has assumed greater importance. A study published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in June 2026 called Trade and Investment in ASEAN in a Fragmented World found that several member states had increased exports of products targeted by US tariffs in 2018-19. Vietnam also attracted significantly more foreign direct investment (FDI) into the affected sectors.
By 2023, ASEAN accounted for more than 20% of American imports of electrical goods, while China’s share fell from more than 40% five years earlier. According to the IMF, the change extends beyond the diversion of trade through third countries; data show an increase in domestically generated value added across ASEAN economies, alongside their continuing reliance on Chinese inputs.
South-East Asia is playing a bigger role in manufacturing within global supply chains. Although tariffs have reduced some direct American imports from China, the US economy remains closely connected to Asia’s manufacturing networks. Parts of those networks have responded by redistributing production and sourcing activities across the region. The difference between economic decoupling and supply chain diversification is important: decoupling seeks to reduce economic ties themselves, whereas diversification aims to limit dependence on any single source.

articles.title: Australia expands export opportunities for Vietnamese goods - Nhan Dan Online
articles.summary: Australia expands export opportunities for Vietnamese goods  Nhan Dan Online
articles.full_text:
Viet Nam and Australia upgraded their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2024. Cooperation agreements between Ho Chi Minh City and the Australian states of Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria, as well as the Northern Territory, have further advanced economic and trade cooperation.
In the first seven months of 2026, bilateral trade between Viet Nam and Australia reached 9.79 billion USD, up 20% compared with the same period in 2025, while Viet Nam's exports to Australia rose by 30%. In Ho Chi Minh City, two-way trade with Australia totalled 1.56 billion USD in the first nine months of 2026. Exports reached 985 million USD, an increase of 16.3% year on year.
Many of Ho Chi Minh City's key product groups have opportunities to enter the Australian market. These include industrial goods, machinery and equipment, textiles and garments, footwear, timber and wood products, agricultural produce, seafood, processedfood and consumer goods. At the same time, the city is seeking cooperation with Australian partners in a range of fields, including technology, logistics, education, clean energy, green development, and other high-value-added industries.
Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Investment and Trade Promotion Centre Le Anh Hoang, said Australia was considered a market with strong purchasing power, diverse demand, and considerable untapped potential for Vietnamese goods. However, it also imposed stringent requirements on product quality, food safety, quarantine and biosecurity, traceability, and technical standards, alongside increasingly demanding sustainability criteria.
To enter and expand in the market effectively, businesses therefore need to proactively improve product quality and thoroughly familiarise themselves with Australian import regulations, consumer trends, distribution networks, and business practices.
According to Hoang, as a major economic, trade, and services hub and one of Viet Nam’s leading gateways for international commerce, Ho Chi Minh City has consistently focused on expanding export markets, diversifying trading partners, and strengthening business links with promising destinations. Australia is among those offering considerable potential for the city's businesses to further develop trade and investment cooperation.
Under its development strategy for 2026–2030, Ho Chi Minh City will continue to promote sustainable import and export activities, increase the added value of goods, accelerate digital and green transformation, develop logistics, and support businesses in integrating more deeply into regional and global supply chains. Expanding cooperation with high-standard markets such as Australia will also encourage businesses in the city to modernise production, improve product quality, and strengthen their competitiveness.
Experts say one of the advantages for Vietnamese businesses in Australia is the three free trade agreements to which both countries are parties: AANZFTA (the ASEAN–Australia–New Zealand Free Trade Area Agreement), CPTPP (the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership), and RCEP (the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership).
Commercial Consul representing the Viet Nam Trade Office in Australia Nguyen Manh Hiep said that amid rising trade protectionism, the reduction of tariffs on most import tariff lines to zero under these agreements helped businesses cut costs and improve their competitiveness.
However, to benefit from these preferences, businesses must comply with rules of origin and prepare all the necessary documentation. Under AANZFTA, they need to understand the rules of origin applicable to each product code, maintain transparent records of input materials, and be prepared to meet verification requests from Australian authorities, including after goods have cleared customs.
 Businesses need to move from simply knowing that FTAs exist to mastering how to use them. This includes restructuring supply chains and maintaining strict control over material sources and documentation.
Nguyen Manh Hiep 
Commercial Consul representing the Viet Nam Trade Office in Australia 
Given this reality, Hiep recommended that businesses move from simply knowing that FTAs exist to mastering how to use them, with a focus on restructuring supply chains and maintaining strict control over material sources and documentation.
Alongside tariff advantages, businesses also face increasingly intense competition. Australian consumers exhibit strong brand loyalty, while Vietnamese goods must compete with products from China, Thailand, and India.
Businesses can broaden their market access through trade fairs and specialised exhibitions, partnerships with local distributors, or cross-border e-commerce for suitable products. For small and medium-sized enterprises, sectoral collaboration is also seen as a way to strengthen supply capacity and meet the requirements of major distribution networks.
According to experts, expanding exports to Australia requires businesses in Ho Chi Minh City to strengthen their capabilities across the board, from production and quality management to supply chain organisation. These are key areas in which the city is focusing its support for businesses seeking to expand imports and exports in conjunction with green and digital transformation, and efforts to enhance product value. This will gradually strengthen businesses' ability to integrate more deeply into international supply chains and markets.

articles.title: Pakistan can benefit from Malaysia’s computer semiconductor manufacturing industry: Envoy - 24 News HD
articles.summary: Pakistan can benefit from Malaysia’s computer semiconductor manufacturing industry: Envoy  24 News HD
articles.full_text:
Malaysia-Pakistan business engagement 2026 highlights trade, investment
Federal Minister for the Board of Investment Qaiser Ahmed Sheikh has said that Pakistan played the role of a peacemaker and mediator in the US-Iran conflict, 24NewsHD TV reported on Friday.
The remarks were made at the Malaysia-Pakistan Business Engagement 2026, organized by the Malaysian High Commission in Islamabad.
The event was attended by representatives of chambers of commerce and industry, business leaders and other stakeholders from both countries. Addressing the gathering, Qaiser Sheikh said Pakistan had effectively defended itself against Indian aggression during Operation Bunyan-um-Marsoos.
He added that Pakistan’s diplomatic role in the US-Iran conflict had been widely appreciated internationally. The federal minister said Pakistan’s strategic geographical location could help Malaysia gain access to the markets of landlocked Central Asian countries. He noted that a resolution of the US-Iran conflict and the lifting of sanctions on Iran could open up a major regional market for Pakistan and Malaysia, encompassing Iran and Central Asia.
Highlighting Pakistan’s economic potential, Sheikh said the country’s large population and substantial domestic market offered significant opportunities for Malaysian businesses. He also expressed the expectation that Malaysia would increase its purchases of Pakistani rice.
Welcoming the participants, Malaysian High Commissioner to Pakistan Dato' Mohammad Azhar Mazlan said Pakistan and Malaysia were among the first Muslim countries to sign a bilateral Free Trade Agreement (FTA).
He announced that the two countries would renew the agreement in the near future. The high commissioner noted that Pakistan was among the four leading buyers of Malaysian palm oil.
He also highlighted Malaysia’s experience in semiconductor manufacturing, saying the country had begun producing computer semiconductors around 30 years ago and had since developed substantial self-sufficiency in the sector.
He said Pakistan could benefit from Malaysia’s expertise and industrial capabilities in semiconductor manufacturing, opening up opportunities for technological cooperation and industrial development between the two countries.
Commenting on regional and international issues, Dato' Mohammad Azhar Mazlan condemned the atrocities committed by Israel in Palestine, particularly in Gaza.
He said Malaysia, like Pakistan, supported a two-state solution to the Palestinian issue.
Sheikh reiterated that Pakistan had never recognized the state of Israel.
During the business engagement, Nadir Ali of MATRADE highlighted the organization’s role in promoting Malaysian trade and strengthening commercial relations with Pakistan.

articles.title: The Ministry of Industry and Trade is closely following the growth scenario and is determined to achieve the targets for 2026. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Ministry of Industry and Trade is closely following the growth scenario and is determined to achieve the targets for 2026.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
After nine months, many indicators in the Industry and Trade sector have met or exceeded targets. The Ministry of Industry and Trade is managing the plan on a monthly basis, aiming for comprehensive achievement of the 2026 goals.
According to data from the Institute for Strategic Studies and Public Policy ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), after nine months of 2026, six out of eight growth targets assigned by the Government to the industry have been met or exceeded. This result is recorded in the context of the national economy maintaining high growth momentum, with GDP in the first nine months estimated to increase by 9.01% compared to the same period last year, the highest level in the past 15 years.
Industrial production continues to affirm its role as the main driver of growth. The Industrial Production Index (IIP) for the first nine months increased by 12.3% compared to the same period last year, the highest increase for the same period since 2019, recording growth in all 34 localities. The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for the manufacturing sector in September reached 51.9 points, continuing to remain above the 50-point threshold, indicating that business conditions in the manufacturing sector continue to improve, although the rate of improvement is slower than the previous month.
Export activities continued to record positive results. Merchandise export turnover in the first nine months reached US$434.30 billion, an increase of 24.5% compared to the same period last year, exceeding the target growth rate of 15-16% set for the whole year. In September alone, the merchandise trade balance recorded a surplus of US$1.27 billion, although the overall trade deficit for the first nine months remained at US$19.42 billion.
The domestic market maintained stable growth. Total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue in the first nine months increased by 13.4% compared to the same period last year. The percentage of businesses applying e-commerce reached 61%. In the energy sector, the power capacity reserve ratio reached approximately 25.97%, 4.17 percentage points higher than the 21.8% figure.
Based on the results of the first nine months, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has updated its growth scenario for the end of 2026. Accordingly, the average growth rate of the industrial production index in the remaining months of the year is expected to reach approximately 12.5 - 13%, ensuring that the whole year falls within the target range of 12 - 14%. Export turnover for the whole year is expected to increase by approximately 22.8%, total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue by approximately 13.3%, while the B2C (business-to-consumer) e-commerce market is expected to grow by approximately 20.5%.
Assessing growth prospects, in an interview with the Industry and Trade Newspaper, Dr. Le Duy Binh, Director of Economica Vietnam, stated that positive results in industrial production, trade, and consumption provide a basis for international organizations to adjust their assessments of Vietnam's economic outlook. Specifically, industrial production maintains high growth momentum, domestic purchasing power remains strong, and exports continue to be a prominent driving force.
The results achieved in the first nine months have laid an important foundation for the Ministry of Industry and Trade to continue pursuing its growth targets for 2026. However, achieving all eight targets comprehensively still requires focused efforts to overcome difficulties, especially for the two targets regarding total power generation capacity and B2C e-commerce growth in the remaining months of the year.
Identifying challenges in the final stretch
You may also like
Despite positive performance results and growth forecasts, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has determined not to be complacent in the face of difficulties and challenges in the remaining months of the year. The results achieved ahead of schedule in the first nine months are considered a safe margin and will not be used to adjust down the operational requirements in the fourth quarter.
First, the international trade environment continues to be fraught with uncertainty. Export activities may face increasing pressure from trade protection measures, changes in tariff policies, and increasingly stringent environmental standards in major markets. Notably, the European Union has entered the formal implementation phase of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which requires businesses to control emissions, meet green standards, and enhance competitiveness.
Domestically, the storm and rainfall in the central region during October and November could affect production, transportation, and supply chains, requiring businesses to proactively develop response plans to minimize disruptions.
Notably, the pressure to achieve targets is concentrated on two priority indicators for the fourth quarter. For the electricity sector, the total power generation capacity currently stands at approximately 85,594.88 MW, requiring an additional 2,570 MW to reach a minimum of 88,165 MW by the end of the year. Meanwhile, the B2C e-commerce market grew by 19.5% after nine months, 0.5 percentage points lower than the lower end of the 20-22% target for the whole year. This necessitates accelerating growth in the remaining months of the year, while also improving the effectiveness of solutions to boost the market.
The above requirements indicate that, in order to build upon the achievements of the past nine months and comprehensively fulfill the 2026 targets, the Ministry of Industry and Trade needs to both maintain growth momentum in areas with positive results and focus on resolving difficulties related to indicators that are lagging behind schedule, ensuring that management is implemented proactively, flexibly, and effectively.
Managed on a monthly basis, with a firm commitment to achieving targets.
According to Official Letter No. 8293/BCT-KHTC dated October 12, 2026, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has established a unified operational scenario aimed at comprehensively achieving all targets for 2026, with a specific roadmap for October, November, and December. A notable point is the application of a three-tiered risk management mechanism (Green, Yellow, Red) for each target. When a target reaches the warning threshold, the lead unit must proactively activate the prepared solutions immediately, without waiting for the quarterly assessment results. In particular, a target must not remain at the Red level for more than one month without a solution and report.
For industrial production, the Ministry of Industry and Trade compiles a list of large enterprises, projects, and localities with large-scale industrial operations to monitor monthly output, prioritizing the assurance of electricity, gas, coal, and raw material supplies for production. At the same time, it urges the progress of bringing new industrial projects into operation in the fourth quarter, maximizing the capacity of oil refineries, fertilizer plants, steel mills, and cement factories to maintain industrial growth momentum in the remaining months of the year.
In the electricity sector, the Ministry of Industry and Trade requires the creation of a list of contingency projects with a total capacity of approximately 3,100 MW, equivalent to no less than 120% of the additional capacity needed. Simultaneously, it calls for accelerating the process of granting commercial operation permits for each unit and each part of the project that meets the requirements; shortening the time for conducting testing and acceptance procedures as stipulated, in order to bring power sources into operation as soon as possible. The Ministry is also proactively developing plans to respond to storms and floods, ensuring coal and gas reserves at power plants, and preparing electricity supply plans for the 2027 dry season.
You may also like
For e-commerce, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is focusing on exploiting year-end shopping peaks and the 2026 Online Friday shopping event, coordinating with major e-commerce platforms to implement programs promoting the consumption of Vietnamese goods, supporting shipping and payment costs. According to the updated scenario, the growth rate of B2C e-commerce in October, November, and December is expected to reach 21%, 23%, and 26% respectively, aiming for a growth target of approximately 20.5% for the whole year.
Alongside promoting transactions, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is strengthening seller verification, ensuring transparency of product information, and managing cross-border e-commerce activities, aiming to build a healthy online business environment and protect consumer rights.
Regarding exports, the focus of management has shifted to maintaining a reasonable growth rate while improving the quality of growth. The Ministry of Industry and Trade is strengthening control over the origin of goods, enhancing the effectiveness of free trade agreements, expanding markets in the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America, and exploiting the potential of the Halal product market. Simultaneously, the Ministry is implementing the "GoGlobal" program for the period 2026-2030, as stipulated in Decision No. 626/QD-TTg of the Prime Minister , to support Vietnamese businesses in expanding their presence in international markets.
For the domestic market, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is focusing on implementing the second national concentrated promotional program, continuing the "Vietnamese people prioritize using Vietnamese goods" campaign, proactively preparing goods for Tet, implementing solutions to stabilize the market, and ensuring a stable supply of petroleum products during the peak period at the end of the year.

articles.title: China looks to ban foreign acquisitions of critical biopharma platforms - Fierce Biotech
articles.summary: China looks to ban foreign acquisitions of critical biopharma platforms  Fierce BiotechChina says it will curb tech exports, including AI, citing national security risks  PBSBeijing seeks tighter grip on AI exports amid US rivalry  ReutersChina Proposes Export Controls on AI Technologies  WSJChina Moves to Restrict Exports of Some Solar Technologies  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
As Washington ramps up efforts to tighten cross-border life sciences deals involving Chinese assets, Beijing is moving to tighten its own grip on biomedical innovation, rolling out a draft policy that would ban or restrict the export of key biopharmaceutical technologies.
In a proposed update to its export blacklist published (Chinese) Friday, China’s government revealed that it is looking to block foreign acquisitions of proprietary cell and gene therapy, small interfering RNA (siRNA) and pathogen gain-of-function platforms. In this case, platforms are defined as sets of reusable technologies that can support the development of multiple drugs.
In parallel, the new rule would restrict the full transfer of proprietary drug target identification and verification technologies in the fields of cell and gene therapy and siRNA to entities overseas. Unlike a full-on ban, a restriction would mean that such deals would require regulatory approval.
Biopharma assets are among 40 key technologies being targeted by the government’s update, which also covers AI and photovoltaic green energy.
The proposed policy comes as China has become a leading exporter of biomedicines. According to China’s drug regulators, foreign transactions of Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion as of August this year, marking a 36% jump year over year.
However, the draft rule’s real impact on Chinese biopharma transactions may be limited.
For biopharma deals, the new regulations can be summarized as “regulating transfers while leaving licensing unconstrained,” Aaron Gu, a partner at Chinese law firm Han Kun that specializes in healthcare and life sciences, told Fierce.
While keen on keeping ownership of key proprietary technologies within China’s borders, the proposed export ban explicitly excludes several common business development types. Out-licensing agreements, as well as utilizing know-how to provide outsourced research and manufacturing services, do not fall under the ban, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Commerce highlighted in a media Q&A (Chinese).
Similarly, out-licensing of drug target identification and verification techs will generally be approved, the spokesperson added.
That describes nearly all Western deals for Chinese biotech assets so far. Despite a surge in deal count and value, U.S. and European biopharma companies and venture capitalists have almost exclusively focused on buying specific drugs from their Chinese counterparts or utilizing a platform to identify new molecules. Rarely has ownership of a platform changed hands.
As of July 1, only five of all 121 cross-border Chinese biopharma out-licensing deals this year involved ownership transfer, according to local biopharma data intelligence service provider PharmCube.
One deal that would likely not have been possible under the proposed new rule was AstraZeneca’s $1 billion acquisition of Gracell Biotechnologies, which developed the FasTCAR platform for making CAR-T cells. When announced at the end of 2023, the deal was hailed as the first full acquisition of a Chinese biotech by Big Pharma.
Explaining the government’s rationale in the Q&A, the spokesperson framed the proposal as supporting the “orderly international collaboration around China’s biopharma technologies.” As for the pathogen-related component, the spokesperson cited national security reasons.
Rumors started circulating in May that the Chinese government was looking to slam the brake on biopharma platform acquisitions. At the time, an alleged Ministry of Commerce blacklist circulating online also proposed platform bans on other popular modalities such as multispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates and protein degraders.
The Chinese government had been surveying research institutions and biopharma companies over the past two years, trying to get a better grasp of the field’s technology landscape, a senior Chinese biopharma executive told Fierce in an interview in June.
The assessment was launched in response to concerns over the practice of out-licensing or selling early-stage drug candidates—coined by locals as “selling green shoots”—because Chinese biotechs lack the experience or the cash to run late-stage clinical trials and global commercialization, the person said.
“What authorities don’t want to see is someone taking China’s resources to build a great R&D engine, only to sell the entire company overseas, because then China ends up losing the capabilities,” the exec said, commenting on the rumor.
“But if you structure it as a partnership, I’m still the owner,” the exec added. “You’re simply licensing it out so foreign companies can develop it overseas while paying you royalties and milestone payments. I don’t think the Chinese government is against that kind of arrangement.”
“Many of these deals retain rights for China—meaning it won’t impact the development and commercialization of these drugs domestically, so Chinese patients still get access to world-class medicines,” the exec continued. “Second, Chinese companies can gain financial returns through these deals, generating foreign exchange for the country. If you think about it from these angles, that’s really the underlying rationale.”
Now, the published draft policy is “significantly better than market expectations,” Gu of Han Kun said.
The previous rumored list “spanned nearly all the most prominent frontiers of Chinese biopharma business development deals,” he observed. “The market had widely feared that Chinese cross-border dealmaking would suffer a sweeping blow.”
“By deliberately excluding out-licensing structures, the government has clearly taken into account biopharma dealmaking norms and the momentum of cross-border collaboration, reflecting strong support from a policy standpoint,” Gu said.
The Chinese government is seeking comments on the proposed new rule until Nov. 15. Foreign buyers should exercise due diligence regarding this draft policy, Gu said. He noted that, before the revised export control catalogue is officially enacted, any export of technologies falling within the regulated scope must register with the Ministry of Commerce.
Beijing is tightening controls over foreign biopharma transactions just as Washington’s China hawks intensify efforts to curb the American purchase of Chinese biotech assets. Congressional Representative John Moolenaar (R-MI), chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Congresswoman Debbie Dingell (D-MI) recently introduced the Biotech Investment National Security Act, looking to put China biopharma deals under additional scrutiny.
However, the draft has not moved forward in Congress. The U.S. Treasury Department, which would be responsible for carrying out the proposed restrictions, is working on rules that would likely preserve U.S. companies’ ability to strike most licensing deals for Chinese drugs, Reuters reported last month, citing three people who have been briefed on the process.
Editor's Note: The story was updated at 2:50 p.m. to include a data point provided by PharmCube.

ACTION:
60-Day notice of extension and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites the general public to take this opportunity to comment on an extension, without change, of a currently approved information collection. In accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this notice seeks comments concerning the Tribal Homeland Security Grant Program (THSGP) investment justification, which allows Indian Tribes to apply for Federal Funding to support efforts to achieve target capabilities related to preventing, preparing for, protecting against, or responding to acts of terrorism.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 15, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To avoid duplicate submissions to the docket, please submit comments at
http://www.regulations.gov
under Docket ID FEMA-2026-0661. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
All submissions received must include the agency name and Docket ID. Regardless of the method used to submit comments or material, all submissions will be posted, without change, to the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
http://www.regulations.gov,
and will include any personal information you provide. Therefore, submitting this information makes it public. You may wish to read the Privacy and Security Notice that is available via a link on the homepage of
http://www.regulations.gov.
The purpose of the THSGP is to make grants available to Federally-recognized “directly eligible tribes,” as defined by section 2005 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (codified as amended at 6 U.S.C. 606), and to provide Tribes with the ability to develop and deliver core capabilities using the combined efforts of the whole community, rather than the exclusive effort of any single organization or level of government. The THSGP's allowable costs support efforts of Tribes to build and sustain core capabilities to prepare for, prevent, protect against, and respond to acts of terrorism. The THSGP also plays an important role in the implementation of the National Preparedness System by supporting the building, sustainment, and delivery of core capabilities essential to achieving FEMA's National Preparedness Goal of a secure and resilient Nation. Federally recognized Tribes are those Tribes appearing on the list published by the Secretary of the Interior pursuant to the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994 (Pub. L. 103-454) (25 U.S.C. 5131). “Directly eligible tribes” are defined in section 2001 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, as amended (Pub. L. 107-296) (6 U.S.C. 601).

articles.title: Treasury Department Issues First Civil Penalty under the Outbound Investment Security Program - JD Supra
articles.summary: Treasury Department Issues First Civil Penalty under the Outbound Investment Security Program  JD Supra
articles.full_text:
On October 7, 2026, the U.S. Department of Treasury announced its first civil enforcement penalty imposed under the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP). For U.S. investment funds, U.S. managers of funds abroad, and U.S. companies with controlled subsidiaries abroad, this enforcement action is a practical reminder that OISP diligence and documentation should extend across controlled foreign entities, including for small and follow-on investments. This is especially relevant to funds investing in Chinese companies in the semiconductor, quantum and artificial intelligence (AI) sectors and U.S. companies with controlled foreign subsidiaries involved with these sectors.
OISP Background
Under the OISP regulations, a covered transaction by a U.S. person involving a person of a country of concern (currently, only China, including Hong Kong and Macau) may be prohibited or notifiable (though certain transactions are excepted). Investments involving AI that are not otherwise prohibited are notifiable if they involve the development of AI systems designed for any military end use, government intelligence, or mass-surveillance end use; intended to be used for cybersecurity applications, digital forensics tools, penetration testing tools, or the control of robotic systems; or trained using certain specified computing thresholds. Investments involving supercomputers, certain quantum computers, quantum computing components and networks, and certain advanced semiconductors are also covered transactions under the current OISP regulations. A summary of investments in the three covered sectors that are prohibited or notifiable is available here.
Critically, the regulations extend to investments made by controlled foreign entities, as was the case in this recent enforcement action. Controlled foreign entities are defined as any foreign entity of which a U.S. person is a parent. Treasury expects U.S. entities to conduct a “reasonable and diligent inquiry” into whether investments may be covered transactions.
Treasury’s First OISP Penalty
Treasury announced its first civil penalty under the OISP regulations against Amidi LLC in the amount of $200,000 for failing to notify Treasury of an investment made on April 19, 2025, by Amidi’s subsidiary, a Chinese fund. The fund, reportedly affiliated with Amidi’s venture capital arm, Plug and Play, invested approximately $92,478 into Shanghai Qiongche Intelligent Technology Company Limited (“Noematrix Ltd.”), a Chinese company developing AI, robotics and embodied intelligence.
Treasury framed the violation as a failure to report a notifiable investment by Amidi’s controlled foreign entity. Notably, the $200,000 penalty is more than twice the reported investment amount. Treasury has not provided its methodology for calculating the penalty, nor has it published a response from Amidi concerning the alleged violation. Under the OISP, Treasury can impose a civil penalty up to $377,700 or an amount that is twice the value of the transaction, whichever is greater.
Treasury stated that it identified the investment through “regular and ongoing compliance and market monitoring efforts,” suggesting it does not rely solely on voluntary self-disclosures or required notifications. It also emphasized that a U.S. person must notify Treasury of transactions by controlled foreign entities when those transactions would be notifiable if undertaken by a U.S. person. A U.S. person must also take all reasonable steps to prevent controlled foreign entities from making prohibited investments.
Looking Ahead
The Amidi penalty shows that even small investments may draw scrutiny when they involve companies, including foreign entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons, engaged in covered activities in China involving AI, semiconductors or quantum. There is no de minimis threshold for the notification requirement, and here, a roughly $92,478 investment by a controlled foreign entity drew a $200,000 penalty.
U.S. funds and investing entities should ensure that diligence and documentation processes are designed to scale as the outbound investment regime expands. As we discussed in a prior alert here, the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025 (“COINS Act”) that became law in December 2025 expands the OSIP to include additional countries and technology sectors. The Department of Treasury is expected to issue rules to implement the COINS Act in the near future.

articles.title: 70 years of China's foreign trade: From 'mutual exchange of goods and services' to global production and supply chain lynchpin - CGTN
articles.summary: 70 years of China's foreign trade: From 'mutual exchange of goods and services' to global production and supply chain lynchpin  CGTN
articles.full_text:
Editor's note: Tian Huifang is a senior research fellow of Institute of World Economics and Politics, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. This article reflects the author's views and not necessarily those of CGTN. It has been translated from Chinese and edited for clarity and brevity.
Workers are busy at a production workshop of a technology engineering equipment company in Guiyang Economic and Technological Development Zone, Guizhou Province, China, October 13, 2026. /VCG
Since the founding of the People's Republic of China more than 70 years ago, the total volume of China's goods trade has soared from about $1.1 billion in 1950 to over $6 trillion in 2025, and its proportion in global trade has also increased from less than 1% to 18.2%. This process has not only reshaped the economic landscape of China, but has also profoundly shaped the division of labor in the global industrial chain and the trajectory of world economic development.
Relying on a complete industrial system and strong manufacturing capabilities, China's manufacturing added value has been ranked first in the world for 15 consecutive years, accounting for nearly 30% of the global total. With over 200 major industrial products produced, China ranks first in the world and is the only country in the world to have all industrial categories classified by the United Nations Industrial Classification. By 2025, China had not only cemented its position as the world's largest trading nation in goods, but also stood as the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's import and export of goods reached 39.94 trillion yuan ($5.8 trillion), a year-on-year increase of 18.8%; Among them, exports amounted to 23.2 trillion yuan, an increase of 16.4%, while imports amounted to 16.74 trillion yuan, an increase of 22.3%. The import growth rate is 5.9 percentage points higher than the export rate, indicating that China is both an important supplier and a continuously expanding global market.
Industrial workers repair a large vessel for export shipping at a private ship repair company at the foot of Chashan Mountain in Rongcheng, Shandong Province, China, October 14, 2026. /VCG
Over the decades, China has exported massive amounts of high-quality and affordable electromechanical products, textiles, and daily consumer goods to the world, meeting the diverse needs of consumers in various countries and significantly enhancing the actual purchasing power of global consumers. During the periods of the epidemic and geopolitical fluctuations, China, with its efficient supply chain resilience, ensured the global supply of medical supplies, key components, and daily consumer goods; effectively alleviated global inflationary pressures; maintained the smoothness and security of the international industrial chain; and played a role as a "stable anchor" and innovation node in the reconstruction of the global industrial chain. At the same time, through the Belt and Road Initiative, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and other initiatives for the global good, China has optimized the global capital allocation, helped host country infrastructure construction and industrial upgrading, and promoted the coordinated development of the regional economy.
While the world has faced increasing unilateralism and trade protectionism in recent years, China has actively participated in WTO reform and the formulation of international economic and trade rules, worked to maintain the multilateral trading system with the WTO as the core, and promoted the development of the global economic governance system toward a more inclusive and balanced direction.
In December 2023, the Central Economic Work Conference of China proposed that China should use disruptive and cutting-edge technologies to stimulate new industries, models, and driving forces, and develop new quality productive forces. Since that time, China's foreign trade has also entered a new stage. Products such as AI, industrial robots, smart wearables, drones, new energy vehicles, energy storage batteries, wind power equipment, new materials, etc. have become new driving forces of China's export growth. Through international trade platforms such as the Canton Fair, they quickly complete product display, demand verification, order conversion, channel construction, and brand promotion.
Wind turbine equipment for export is prepared for loading at the Dongfang Port Company terminal of Lianyungang Port in Lianyungang, Jiangsu Province, China, October 13, 2026. /VCG
By 2025, China's high-tech product exports had reached 5.25 trillion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 13.2%. Among them, the export scale of "new three types" (new energy vehicles, lithium batteries, photovoltaic products) products was close to 1.3 trillion yuan, an increase of 3.5 times compared to 2020. In the first three quarters of 2026, the equipment manufacturing industry contributed nearly 90% of the export growth, integrated circuit exports increased by 99.1%, and exports of electric vehicles, lithium batteries, wind turbines, and parts increased by 72.3%, 36.4%, and 22.4%, respectively. At the 2026 Autumn Canton Fair, new quality productivity representative products such as intelligent robots, high-end equipment, and green building materials will get much visibility and gain significant attention. All these factors and developments indicate that the driving force of China's trade growth is shifting from traditional cost advantages to new advantages such as technology, quality, green attributes, and industrial supporting capabilities.
For China's foreign trade, new quality productivity is not just about improving the technological content of exported products, but also about the systematic changes in production factors, production tools, industrial organization, and business models.
On the one hand, artificial intelligence, industrial internet, 5G, robots and digital production lines have improved the R&D, production, quality control and flexible manufacturing capabilities of enterprises, enabling enterprises to respond more quickly to the small batch, personalized and scenario needs of consumers in different countries.
On the other hand, new energy, new materials, energy storage, green manufacturing, and circular economy promote the low-carbon development of export products, enabling Chinese enterprises to participate in global energy transformation and green industry chain reconstruction.
In addition, cross-border e-commerce, digital marketing, overseas warehouses, and intelligent logistics have compressed the time for innovative products to enter overseas markets, allowing small and medium-sized enterprises to no longer rely solely on traditional large traders, but to have more direct contact with overseas consumers and professional buyers.
As the main force of foreign trade, more and more private enterprises are no longer satisfied with simple processing, but are transforming from "product going global" to "brand going global" and "industry chain going global" through independent research and development, independent brand building, and independent channel construction.
The flourishing development of new formats such as cross-border e-commerce, overseas warehouses, and bonded maintenance has further expanded the boundaries of China's trade.

Automakers work at full capacity to fulfill domestic and international orders in Liuzhou, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China, October 12, 2026. /VCG
Overall, the contribution of China's foreign trade to the world economy does not rest solely on export volume expansion, but manifests itself more in technological cooperation, import expansion, transparent rules, brand building, green development, and support for industrialization in developing countries. Looking toward the future, with the continuous release of new quality productivity, China's foreign trade will pay more attention to quality, efficiency, and innovation. With the help of high-level open platforms such as the Canton Fair, China will continue to meet global demand with high-quality supply, promote industrial upgrading through technological innovation, maintain global industrial chain stability through open cooperation, and inject more certainty and positive energy into the development of the world economy.

articles.title: Nippon Express Holdings Acquires Metro Supply Chain Group to Expand North American Logistics Operations - citybiz
articles.summary: Nippon Express Holdings Acquires Metro Supply Chain Group to Expand North American Logistics Operations  citybiz
articles.full_text:
Nippon Express Holdings, Inc. (NX Group), a Japan-based global logistics company, has completed its acquisition of all outstanding shares of Metro Supply Chain Group Inc., a Montreal-based contract logistics provider, strengthening its North American operations and expanding its international warehousing, fulfillment and distribution capabilities.
The transaction closed on October 1, 2026, with NX Group assuming full ownership of Metro Supply Chain Group. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.
The companies marked the completion of the transaction with an employee town hall meeting and closing ceremony in Montreal on October 7, attended by NX Group President and CEO Satoshi Horikiri and Metro Supply Chain Group founder and Group Chairman Chiko Nanji.
The acquisition establishes Metro Supply Chain Group as a central component of NX Group’s global contract logistics strategy, providing an operating platform for expansion across North America and the transfer of advanced fulfillment and warehouse automation capabilities to other international markets.
Headquartered in Montreal, Metro Supply Chain Group operates primarily in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom, providing contract logistics services across a diversified customer base.
Its operations serve retail, consumer goods, automotive and manufacturing, healthcare and wellness, technology and services, and public sector customers.
The company specializes in managing logistics functions for businesses that outsource warehousing, inventory management, order fulfillment and distribution operations.
By acquiring Metro Supply Chain Group, NX Group intends to strengthen its regional logistics infrastructure while expanding its ability to provide integrated supply chain services to multinational customers.
The transaction supports NX Group’s strategy of developing a broader contract logistics business alongside its established international transportation and freight forwarding operations.
Contract logistics services typically involve longer-term arrangements under which providers manage warehousing, inventory handling, order processing and distribution activities on behalf of customers.
These operations can complement international freight transportation by connecting the movement of goods across borders with their storage, processing and delivery within regional markets.
Metro Supply Chain Group’s established operations give NX Group additional capabilities in these areas, particularly in North America.
The acquisition also provides access to Metro Supply Chain Group’s fulfillment processes and warehouse automation technologies, which NX Group plans to introduce across its broader international network.
These capabilities include systems and operating methods supporting order processing, inventory management and shipping.
NX Group intends to use Metro Supply Chain Group as a core platform for developing its contract logistics operations globally, with particular emphasis on applying its expertise in Europe and Asia.
The company also plans to evaluate opportunities to incorporate Metro Supply Chain Group’s operating methods into existing NX Group facilities and customer operations.
This approach is intended to improve operational efficiency and strengthen the company’s ability to manage complex distribution requirements across different markets.
The integration strategy extends beyond warehouse operations to include cross-selling opportunities between the two companies’ customer bases.
NX Group plans to offer international transportation services to Metro Supply Chain Group customers that require freight movement between countries or regions.
At the same time, the company intends to develop additional freight forwarding and customs brokerage relationships through customers already using Metro Supply Chain Group’s contract logistics services.
The strategy is designed to connect warehousing and distribution relationships with international freight transportation and customs services.
For customers, the combined operations could provide access to a wider range of supply chain services through the same corporate group.
These services may include international shipping, customs clearance, inventory management, warehousing, fulfillment and regional distribution.
NX Group expects the combination to support customers seeking greater coordination between their international transportation requirements and domestic logistics operations.
The acquisition also expands the company’s presence in markets where Metro Supply Chain Group has established customer relationships and operating infrastructure.
During the October 7 ceremony, Horikiri and Nanji discussed NX Group’s strategic direction with Metro Supply Chain Group’s management and employees.
The event emphasized the companies’ plans to coordinate operations and pursue growth opportunities across North America and international markets.
NX Group said the combined organization will focus on developing customer relationships, expanding logistics capabilities and identifying opportunities to improve operations through the exchange of technology and expertise.
The transaction brings together NX Group’s international logistics network and Metro Supply Chain Group’s contract logistics operations, creating opportunities to serve customers requiring both cross-border transportation and domestic fulfillment services.
For Metro Supply Chain Group, the acquisition provides access to NX Group’s global infrastructure and international transportation capabilities.
For NX Group, the transaction adds an established contract logistics business with operations in three major markets and experience serving a broad range of industries.
The companies have not disclosed Metro Supply Chain Group’s annual revenue, employee count, total warehouse space or the number of facilities included in the acquisition.
NX Group also has not announced specific financial synergy targets, integration costs or a timetable for implementing Metro Supply Chain Group’s warehouse automation technologies across its international operations.
The acquisition nevertheless represents a significant expansion of NX Group’s contract logistics platform and its North American operating presence.
By combining Metro Supply Chain Group’s fulfillment and distribution expertise with NX Group’s international transportation network, the company intends to develop more integrated supply chain offerings while expanding its contract logistics business across Europe, Asia and North America.
The next phase will focus on coordinating customer services, identifying cross-selling opportunities and applying operational technologies across the combined logistics network.
