articles.title: Germany's draft Investment Screening Act: Implications for cross-border transactions explained - Freshfields
articles.summary: Germany's draft Investment Screening Act: Implications for cross-border transactions explained  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
A key area of changes deals with the question of what level of influence on German companies is significant enough to become notifiable – including a readjustment of voting rights thresholds, and expansions of the catch-all concepts of “atypical influence” and circumvention. Another change affects all situations in which a company holds shares on account of someone else. These changes are intended to close alleged “gaps” in the Ministry’s screening net.
Tailored voting thresholds
Standard initial screening triggers remain at 10% (for defence and critical infrastructure) and 25% (for other sensitive sectors). Subsequent acquisitions will trigger reviews at 50%, 75%, and a new 100% threshold, which captures full buyouts from existing majority control. The intermediate 20% and 40% thresholds will be abolished. This removes unnecessary regulatory friction and simplifies incremental stake-building in private companies. For publicly traded companies, the draft introduces dedicated thresholds of 15% and 30%. The 30% threshold is inspired by German takeover law and the 15% threshold captures anchor stakes that often confer de facto influence due to low attendance at annual general meetings. Furthermore, the Ministry is empowered to establish, by statutory ordinance, differing or additional screening thresholds.
The draft also introduces a new 100% threshold. This is unprecedented; under current law, the highest statutory threshold is 75%. This provision would be applicable to all companies, not just listed companies. From a corporate governance and security perspective, this new threshold appears to make little sense. Once an investor holds 75% of the voting rights, any blocking minority under German corporate law is already eliminated. The shareholder already exercises complete strategic control. For listed companies with an initial 15% threshold, an 85% threshold would mirror the loss of a 15% blocking stake. Pushing the threshold all the way to 100%, however, appears to lack substantive justification. Instead, it creates an unnecessary regulatory hurdle for routine corporate clean-ups, minority buyouts, and statutory squeeze-outs where no additional control is gained.
Atypical influence decoupled from voting stakes
Atypical influence is a concept that allows the Ministry to treat board seats, veto rights, or information rights like voting shares if they grant comparable influence.
The draft sensibly renames ‘atypical control’ to ‘atypical influence’, appropriately reflecting that these cases by no means involve an acquisition of corporate control. The current test requires the acquisition of at least some voting rights alongside additional influence. The draft expands this so that securing board seats, strategic veto rights, or sensitive information access can trigger review even without acquiring any voting rights. In the view of the Ministry this closes a loophole which, according to the Ministry, was previously used to avoid review. But by triggering screening without any share purchase, the draft removes investment control from the M&A process. Instead of screening transactions, it effectively creates a permanent, ongoing review of routine corporate governance.
Asset deals and IP licensing
The Draft IPG clarifies the perimeter of covered asset transactions, confirming that the acquisition of essential business assets “in whole or in substantial part” or significant domestic real estate triggers review. 
Crucially for the tech sector, the draft refrains from introducing a general, standalone screening trigger for licence agreements. Commercial licences will not be caught. Licensing arrangements will only face screening if the licensed intellectual property constitutes the target’s essential operational assets or if the structure serves to circumvent the rules.
Expansive ‘object or effect’ anti-circumvention rule 
The anti-circumvention rule has long been a key priority for the Ministry, which has grown increasingly frustrated with deal structures designed to sit just below statutory thresholds for purported tax or commercial reasons. While the Ministry previously had to prove that parties acted with a deliberate intent to evade investment screening, the Draft IPG now introduces an objective “object and effect test”. Going forward, the Ministry will no longer need to demonstrate that the parties acted with the deliberate intent to avoid review; it will be sufficient that the transaction structure objectively results in evading review. 
Read literally, the new provision could have an extremely broad scope of application as many – completely legitimate transaction structures – could have as their “effect” that German investment screening law is not applicable. The draft offers little guidance on where the line will be drawn. Although the Ministry drew inspiration from European antitrust law, competition case law will be of limited help in practice, as the standard is applied here in an entirely different context. 
Transactions most likely to attract scrutiny under this rule include the divergence of capital and voting rights and synthetic control structures. Dealmakers can no longer take comfort simply from staying under the percentage triggers if the deal effectively bypasses screening in practice.
Holding voting rights “on account” of someone else
Under the draft IPG, the investment screening regime would also cover situations in which a person holds voting rights “on account” of someone else. According to the draft’s explanatory memorandum, voting rights are attributed to whoever bears the “economic risk” of the investment, presuming that economic exposure translates into actual voting influence. The memorandum explicitly confirms that this covers both trustee arrangements and fund structures. Phrased so broadly, this may trigger mandatory filings for passive financial capital, which should not be in the Ministry’s own interest. Beyond these expressly cited examples, the exact scope of this provision is not clear in practice It remains open how this rule will be applied to capital market instruments such as depositary receipts, total return swaps, or synthetic equity, where investors bear economic risk without holding governance or voting rights.

articles.title: How Indian space tech startups are going global and attracting foreign capital - Forbes India
articles.summary: How Indian space tech startups are going global and attracting foreign capital  Forbes India
articles.full_text:
In October, just three months after becoming the first private Indian space tech startup to launch a rocket in space, Skyroot is fielding enquiries from abroad about its launch vehicle Vikram.“Seventy to 80 percent of the demand we are seeing is global,” says Pawan Chandana, its co-founder and CEO. 
Most enquiries have been from the US, Europe and Southeast Asia. In October, Skyroot teamed up with Brazil’s Concert Technologies to jointly develop a 100-kg low Earth orbit launch vehicle, while also securing a deal with US-based Reflect Orbital to deploy future spacecraft across two dedicated launches.This global interest is matched by a surge in foreign capital. Not just in Skyroot.
Pixxel, a Bengaluru-based startup that works on Earth imaging satellites, closed a $100 million round in September, the largest the sector has seen, led by global investment firms Temasek and Seraphim. The company was also the first Indian space tech startup to raise from a global investor when Canada’s Radical Ventures led its Series A, and in 2023, Google made its first ever investment in an Indian space tech startup by leading Pixxel’s $36 million Series B. In 2021, Agnikul Cosmos, a launch vehicle startup, raised $11 million in a Series A round led by Mayfield India, the India-focussed arm of US-based Mayfield.
Indian startups are also embedding themselves into foreign markets. Digantara, a space surveillance and intelligence company, has established a manufacturing and operational footprint in Denver, Colorado, purpose-built to service US government and defence contracts. Its other such facility abroad is in Singapore. 
Beyond drawing foreign capital and sewing up foreign contracts, India’s space tech startups are also building unique technologies. GalaxEye became the first Indian space tech startup to secure a landmark US patent for its OptoSAR in September, a proprietary dual-sensor technology that integrates optical and radar observation. This does not exist anywhere else in the world and is getting interest from clients in West Asia.The task now is to convert this attention into commercial success, mass production, and, eventually, sustainable global market share. The upside is huge. The global space economy is put at $630 billion, according to an estimate by World Economic Forum and McKinsey & Company in 2023, and the US accounts for most of it, followed by China, Europe and Japan. India accounts for less than 2 percent, with its space tech sector estimated at $8.4 billion.
Global Play
India opened up its space sector to private participation long after the US and Europe did. However, this does not faze Pawan Goenka, chairman of IN-SPACe, a government agency for promoting private space tech industry. “Our companies are quite aggressive in wooing customers outside India,” he says, adding that India’s startups are winning orders from abroad and “will be very competitive in two to three years”. 
IN-SPACe data shows that only half of India’s top 10 space tech companies lean heavily on the home market. MistEO gets all its orders from domestic entities, Suhora and GalaxEye above 90 percent, Digantara 80 percent, and Bellatrix more than 70 percent.The other five look outward. Dhruva Space gets 90 percent of its business from abroad and HEX20 80 percent. Agnikul describes most of its orders as international and Skyroot says its book is predominantly foreign. Piersight sits in the middle, with half of its business being international.Firms selling launch vehicles and launch-linked services skew global, while those that depend on Indian government and defence customers stay anchored at home. The overseas orders are mostly for hardware and engineering services rather than data. They include satellite structures, solar panels, propulsion systems, and full satellites and design work, which suggests Indian startups are winning abroad as low-cost, space-qualified suppliers. 
Companies focussed on data and analytics find that orders from overseas require more than hardware exports.Pixxel, for instance, is building a physical presence in the markets where it sells. It has a subsidiary in El Segundo, California, which CEO Awais Ahmed credits with winning the Nasa and National Reconnaissance Office contracts—a $476 million Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme, giving the hyperspectral imaging startup a route to supply Earth observation data to the US space agency till November 2028.
A European subsidiary is “on the verge”, Ahmed says, with West Asia and Southeast Asia to follow. The European national governments, the EU and the European Space Agency have all raised their budgets, he says, creating room for unique space products such as hyperspectral imagery. Revenue, he argues, should be diversified not only between government and commercial customers but also across governments. What gets Pixxel through the door, he adds, is technology no one else offers at that resolution, “because if you are just replicating something that someone else has already done, it becomes difficult”. Pixxel is also planning to go public soon, Ahmed says.Mark Boggett, CEO of Seraphim, the global venture capital firm dedicated to space tech which led Pixxel’s record funding round in September, frames Pixxel’s model as a template for Indian startups to transition from being domestic players to competing globally. He points out how it “has built significant technology and manufacturing capabilities in India while establishing operations in the US, giving it access to customers, talent and capital in the world’s largest space market”. Boggett predicts that the next five to 10 years could be decisive, and that India’s engineering talent, government ambition and growing private funding will “create the conditions for companies to emerge that can compete globally”.
The World Knows
Digantara’s international strategy focuses on Asian markets first. It set up a wholly owned subsidiary in Singapore in 2022 and used the city state as a gateway to Asia-Pacific, finding clients in Thailand and Japan. Anirudh Sharma, CEO of Digantara, says India’s Ministry of External Affairs has helped open doors in places such as the Philippines and Mongolia, where Digantara wants to site ground sensors. Madagascar is next. “These countries are so small that no big company will look at them,” he says, “but they are good enough markets for us to start with.” 
It is not a bad start. Digantara has gone on to hold US government contracts for space situational awareness and missile defence, and bought a 30,000 square foot facility in Denver; the company’s facility in Bengaluru spans 50,000 square feet.“Most of the US government customers, including the Pentagon, know of us and have worked with us,” says Sharma, adding that these are multiple contracts ranging from building payloads to designing algorithms, from software to building a spacecraft.Digantara’s American subsidiary is staffed by US citizens and operates independently of its Indian parent; it is run day to day by US citizens who make operational decisions. This helps it work with US government customers and comply with rules on foreign access to sensitive technology. 
That is a requirement of the work and also a limit. “We cannot have any control over the entity… it has to be an independent entity with no influence from India because we work on national security for the US government,” Sharma says.
Skyroot’s Chandana says clients from Europe and Southeast Asia, in addition to the US, are creating demand across Earth observation, communications, Internet of Things (IoT), climate and weather monitoring, technology demonstrations, and other emerging small-satellite applications.
“The larger opportunity for Vikram (Skyroot’s small satellite rocket) is around dedicated and responsive access to space.
Many small-satellite operators today have to fly as secondary payloads on larger rockets.
That can mean waiting for availability and compromising on the timing or precise orbit they require,” he explains.
Echoing the need for reliable access, Reflect Orbital Co-founder and CEO Ben Nowack says, “There’s a real launch capacity shortage right now.
We’re excited to work with a new launch provider, Skyroot, to help ensure access to space.
”Chennai-based Agnikul’s Srinath Ravichandran describes a quieter European presence.
Agnikul has signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoU) with European players.
“We have announced a few of these publicly,” he says of the MoUs with Finnish company ICEYE for launching synthetic aperture radar Earth observation systems from India, and with France’s Safran in June.
“Some others are still confidential.
”His company plans to fly its reusable Agnibaan rocket in 2027 and has seen interest from imaging satellite operators in Europe and Australia, and from communications operators in Europe, Japan and Australia.
Ravichandran describes a shift in how overseas buyers see India.
“The world knows that we know what it means to build space-grade systems,” he says, a reputation he credits to Isro’s decades of work.

Other companies have taken different routes.
Different Orbits
Bellatrix says 85 to 90 percent of its revenue is exports, mostly to European customers. Its propulsion systems are bought by constellation operators planning multiple satellites, none of which can function without a propulsion system. Rohan Ganapathy, co-founder, CEO and CTO, says the startup is also looking east, not just geographically but also with an entirely new piece of hardware. Its push into Asia bets on a new satellite built for very low Earth orbit (VLEO), where hardly anyone has managed to stay up.It has a collaboration with South Korea’s Telepix, an imaging firm, to fly a wide-swath camera in VLEO, around 200 km above Earth. The orbit is unusual because it is where satellites normally cannot stay. articles.title: France and Germany reach agreement on the future of the European automotive industry. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: France and Germany reach agreement on the future of the European automotive industry.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to the Vietnam News Agency correspondent in Paris, France and Germany reached a significant agreement on October 15th regarding the future of the European automotive industry, easing emissions reduction requirements from 2035 while tightening criteria prioritizing products manufactured in Europe.
 The compromise between the two largest economies in the European Union (EU) is expected to resolve long-standing disagreements over automotive policy, amid increasing competitive pressure on the industry from China .
 According to diplomatic sources on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels, Belgium, on the same day, Paris has agreed to concessions from Berlin on CO2 emissions standards for cars from 2035. In return, Germany agreed to France's request to apply stricter criteria to products recognized as "Made in Europe."
 This is a significant step forward after months of negotiations between the two countries, which have differing priorities in their automotive industry development policies.
 While France wants to strengthen regional production protection and promote the transition to electric vehicles , Germany is particularly interested in maintaining the operation of its internal combustion engine factories, protecting jobs, and preserving the competitiveness of its automotive industry.
 The new agreement stipulates that car manufacturers must reduce CO2 emissions by 90% by 2035, but no longer have the obligation to offset the remaining 10% as initially proposed by the European Commission (EC). This adjustment is justified by the prospect of increasingly widespread use of renewable fuels, including biofuels.
 If approved, the new regulations would further facilitate the development and sale of hybrid vehicles—cars that combine an internal combustion engine with an electric motor—after 2035.
 This is one of the key demands that Berlin is pursuing to protect the traditional automotive industry, especially large corporations like Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz.
 Previously, the EU had set a target of reducing CO2 emissions from new cars by 100% by 2035, which would effectively mean ending the sale of new cars powered by conventional petrol and diesel engines.
 However, in light of the automotive industry's difficulties, in December 2025, the EC proposed reducing the requirement to 90%, on the condition that manufacturers offset the remaining emissions through solutions such as using low-emission steel or sustainable fuels. The Franco-German compromise further relaxed this proposal by removing the offsetting obligation.
 In return, Berlin agreed to narrow the scope of the European product preference principle in the automotive sector. Accordingly, vehicles eligible for preferential treatment must meet production criteria in the 27 EU member states or certain close partner countries, including the UK and Norway .
 The "Made in Europe" principle is part of the EU's industrial promotion bill, requiring businesses in strategic sectors, when receiving public funding, to prioritize the use of components manufactured in Europe or in partner countries that meet certain conditions.
 Previously, Germany advocated the concept of "Made with Europe," allowing for the expansion of priority areas to include countries outside the EU. Berlin argued that the automotive supply chain is highly international and that overly restrictive production scopes could increase costs and negatively impact the competitiveness of businesses.
 Meanwhile, France wants industrial support funds to directly boost production and create jobs in Europe. 
 A notable point in this compromise is France's acceptance of including the UK within the scope of partners eligible for preferential treatment.
 According to the Financial Times on October 15, the joint proposal from Paris and Berlin stipulates that the UK must adopt corresponding EU trade protection measures, particularly tariffs on electric cars imported from China.
 Currently, the EU applies tariffs of up to 45% on some Chinese electric vehicle models, while the UK maintains an import tariff of 10%.
 Whether London will agree to adjust its trade policies in order to participate in the EU's preferred manufacturing scheme remains to be negotiated.
 The Franco-German agreement comes as the European automotive industry faces profound changes. Traditional manufacturers must both invest heavily in transitioning to electric vehicles and compete with Chinese automakers who have advantages in pricing, battery technology, and product development speed.
 According to The Financial Times, the market share of Chinese brands in the EU plug-in hybrid vehicle market has increased from around 2% in 2024 to 25% in the first half of 2026.
 At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, the increasing presence of Chinese automakers also reflects the competitive pressure on established European manufacturers.

articles.title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Shortraker Rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska
articles.summary: NMFS is prohibiting retention of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA) except by catcher/ processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. This action is necessary because the 2026 shortraker rockfish total allowable catch (TAC) in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA for vessels other than Central GOA Rockfish Program catcher/processors will soon be or has been reached.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
                    SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting retention of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA) except by catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. This action is necessary because the 2026 shortraker rockfish total allowable catch (TAC) in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA for vessels other than Central GOA Rockfish Program catcher/processors will soon be or has been reached.
                    DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 14, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the GOA (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The 2026 shortraker rockfish TAC in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA for vessels other than catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit is 113 metric tons as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish of the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS has determined that the 2026 TAC of shortraker rockfish for vessels other than catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit will soon be or has been reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(2), NMFS is prohibiting retention of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA and requiring that shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA be treated in the same manner as a prohibited species, as described under § 679.21(a)(2), for the remainder of the year, except for shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA caught by catcher vessels using hook-and-line, pot, or jig gear as described in § 679.20(j) or caught by catcher vessels using trawl gear participating in the electronic monitoring program as described in § 679.21(a)(2). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 shortraker rockfish TAC in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA. This action does not apply to catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. While this prohibition is effective the requirements of § 679.20(j)(4) apply.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data in a timely fashion and would delay prohibiting the retention of shortraker rockfish for vessels other than catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on the total catch of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 13, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.
                    
                    
                        16 U.S.C. 1801 
                        et seq.
                
                    Dated: October 14, 2026.
Shannon Bettridge,
Acting Director, Office of Sustainable Fisheries, National Marine Fisheries Service.

articles.title: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz - CNBC
articles.summary: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz  CNBCTwo ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles amid surge in attacks  ReutersIran Guards say oil tanker exploded after hitting mine in 'unauthorized' route through Hormuz  The Times of IsraelShips in Strait of Hormuz still face "indiscriminate attacks," maritime monitor warns  CBS NewsShip attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports ...
articles.full_text:
Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and lucrative shipping opportunities keep some operators willing to brave escalating attacks, maritime experts said.
The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away.
Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats.
"I don't see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity," Koh told CNBC.
His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe.
Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents.
Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran's continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation.
Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs.
Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages.
Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said.
Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers.
Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called "Hormuz shuttle" involving about 20 very large crude carriers.
The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official's account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks.
"Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the 'Hormuz shuttle,'" Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying.
Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said.
However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies' assessments of the risks, he added.
The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions.
"Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy," said association president TS Teo.
Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added.
While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait.
Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels.
That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said.
However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman's Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries.
"If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them," Krishna said.

articles.full_text:
Guangzhou, October 14, 2026
Distinguished Guests,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
Friends,
It is a great pleasure to join you in the beautiful Flower City Guangzhou for the 140th Session of China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair). On behalf of the Chinese government, I would like to extend a warm welcome to you all, and express heartfelt appreciation for your long-standing, positive contribution to the economic and trade cooperation and development between China and other countries.
This year marks the 70th anniversary of the Canton Fair. President Xi Jinping has sent a congratulatory letter to the Fair, acknowledging its past achievements and reaffirming China’s commitment to expanding high-standard opening up. Over the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has grown from strength to strength. Its exhibition area has expanded from 9,600 square meters in the first year to 1.55 million square meters today. The number of buyers has increased from 1,200 in the beginning to more than 300,000 this year. Among all the international trade exhibitions hosted by China, the Canton Fair has the longest history, the largest participation and the highest transaction volume. It is also an important window for the international community to observe China. Through this window, the world has witnessed the surging vitality of China’s economy and society, the enterprising journey undertaken by hundreds of millions of Chinese people, and the deepening connection between China and the world.
First, a China that keeps opening itself creates new opportunities for the world. Over the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has established itself and thrived on openness. Its circle of friends has grown bigger, with buyers coming from over 220 countries and regions, and the total value of business deals reaching US$1.6 trillion. What underlies this success is China’s strategic choice of boosting development through openness, and the practical need for countries around the world to leverage their economic strengths for mutual empowerment. China is now a key trading partner of over 160 countries and regions, and the top export destination for nearly 80 countries and regions. China’s stock of overseas investment has reached US$3.4 trillion. While developing itself, China has also brought benefits to the world.
Second, a China that keeps innovating itself provides new impetus for the world. Over the past 70 years, exhibits at the Canton Fair have been continuously transformed and upgraded. From agricultural and subsidiary products and local specialties in the 1960s and 70s, to industrial and electromechanical products in the 1980s and 90s, and to embodied artificial intelligence (AI) and smart medical services today, each session of the Canton Fair presents an updated selection of exhibits. What underlies this transformation is China’s rapid progress in innovation-driven development, and the world’s scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation. In recent years, new technologies, products and business forms in such areas as AI, green energy and biomedicine have continued to emerge in China, and generated new dynamism and space for the world economy.
Third, a China that always keeps its promise brings certainty to the world. Over the past 70 years, no matter how the international situation evolved, the Canton Fair has never been interrupted, and its commitment to the principle of honoring contracts and maintaining credibility remains steadfast. What underlies such commitment is the Chinese philosophy of matching words with actions, and the world’s recognition of and trust in China. China has all along kept its policies stable and consistent, firmly delivered on its commitment of lowering tariffs, increasing development assistance and addressing climate change, and undertaken the responsibilities of a major country in this turbulent and changing world.
Looking back on the past 70 years, the Canton Fair has stood the test of international vicissitudes and brimmed with new vigor and vitality. This is because it has all along followed the trend of economic globalization and answered the call of the international community for joint development. The journey of the Canton Fair offers some simple yet profound takeaways worthy of deep reflection. Here, I would like to share with you three main observations.
First, market connectivity is not a tool for zero-sum games between countries, but an effective measure to foster new space for growth. The past few years have seen a notable rise in manmade market barriers of various sorts around the globe. Some have even chosen to politicize, instrumentalize, and weaponize economic and trade issues. However, no matter their forms, protectionism is always at the core. It has been fully proven by both theories and practices that the market is not static—it is more like a network that reaches out in all directions. Only when connected to more such networks, can a market achieve economy of scale, match supply with demand more efficiently, and create more value and space. Protectionism may seem effective for a country to sustain its market, but it also makes it impossible for the country to broaden its market. Worse still, it may even lose its place in the new global network of markets. At the end of the day, protectionism will only produce more losses than gains.
Throughout the years, China has been committed to integrating its domestic market with the international markets for joint growth. China has been the second largest importer in the world for 17 consecutive years, exceeding RMB 18 trillion yuan last year, and growing by another 22.3 percent in the first three quarters this year. Decades have passed since China opened itself to the world, yet its market has not contracted. Instead, the introduction of new products and industries from other countries, such as automobiles and home appliances, has unlocked and cultivated new market demands. Meanwhile, the export of quality Chinese products, especially innovative products, is opening up new space for the global marketplace. China is ready to work with all countries to build an open world economy and strengthen market connectivity so as to make the global market bigger and deliver greater benefits to all.
Second, international trade is not just statistics in the books, but a voluntary choice aimed to improve people’s well-being. Recently, there have been quite some discussions about the issue of trade balance globally. The laws of economics tell us that a balanced position in trade is temporary and relative, while an imbalanced position is more common and non-static. This is determined by countries’ differences in comparative strengths, economic structures, distribution of labor, and other variables. We need to see that trade is mutually beneficial in nature. One cannot simply view surplus as “taking advantage” and deficit as “being ripped off.” A balanced trade would naturally arrive when the parties can satisfy their respective demands through positive interactions. It is not achieved by building walls, setting up barriers, or even suppressing and containing others. It is simply unrealistic to impose export control on others while looking for balanced trade at the same time. Such a practice will only push up costs, disrupt industrial and supply chains, and further aggravate the imbalance. What we need is “upward balance” achieved by opening up wider and making the economic pie bigger, not “downward balance” resulting from market closure and the inevitable market contraction that follows.
Some current discussions about China’s trade focus on import and export statistics, but overlook the real effects behind them.
China is both a “super seller” and a “super buyer.
” As a “super seller,” China brings benefits to its trading partners.
Quality, affordable goods made by diligent Chinese workers with their labor and wisdom have significantly increased the actual purchasing power of global consumers, improved their quality of life, and helped countries strengthen their capacity for industrial development.
As a “super buyer,” China helps to boost the prosperity of other countries.
China is a major buyer of agricultural, industrial, and consumer goods from many countries, which translate into profits for local businesses, income for the people, and revenues for the governments.
China never seeks surplus intentionally, not to mention the fact that most of the times, the benefits are shared by all parties, despite the surplus being recorded in China.
A large number of foreign-invested enterprises in China export their products across the world and secure big returns.
We would like to buy more products from across the world, especially high value-added products.
Since last year, we have hosted around 70 events themed “Big Market for All: Export to China.
” Next month, we will host the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai.
China hopes that more countries will work together in the same direction, lift restrictions, and pursue better, balanced development of trade.

Third, win-win cooperation does not mean one-sided concession but mutual empowerment and success. On the path toward global prosperity and development, win-win cooperation is the only right choice. A zero-sum approach hurts everybody. For true win-win cooperation to happen, we cannot rely on a simple quid pro quo, still less compromise or concessions under pressure. What we need is to treat each other as equals, meet each other halfway, and make progress together. With all the links of global industrial and supply chains interlocked and closely connected, it is possible to realize more sustainable win-win cooperation at a higher level if countries work together in good faith and draw on each other’s strengths. In this process, developed countries should take more proactive actions, provide developing countries with more capital and technological support and preferential economic and trade policies t

articles.title: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the context of increasingly fierce competition to attract foreign investment, India is linking incentives to revenue, domestic supply chains, and R&D activities. This approach is noteworthy as Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies to better align with project performance.
India is spending $7.5 billion, but not just to produce more phones.
On August 21, 2026, India announced the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme 2026 (MPMS), following the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme which ended on March 31.
During the four years of implementing the PLI (Private Partnership in the Mobile Industry), from 2022 to 2025, India's smartphone exports increased more than sevenfold, from $3.1 billion to $24.1 billion. By 2025, smartphones will become the country's largest export item. This result lays the foundation for India to move to the next phase in its mobile phone industry development strategy.
Instead of focusing solely on expanding manufacturing and assembly, India aims to become a global mobile phone manufacturing and export hub, while also integrating the domestic supply chain more deeply into the process. The MPMS (Mobile Manufacturing and Production Management System) is designed to link the growth of production and revenue for businesses with the use of domestically sourced components as well as design, research, and development (R&D) activities.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
A notable aspect of MPMS is that support is determined based on the actual performance of the business. For large-scale manufacturers, the support amount is calculated based on the portion of revenue exceeding the standard revenue threshold. Businesses that reach a certain revenue threshold and continue to maintain growth will be eligible for support.
This mechanism also encourages businesses to increase their use of components sourced from the Indian market. Phones using domestically sourced components can receive an additional subsidy of up to 1.5%. These components include screens, cameras, phone casings, batteries, and charging cables.
Indian domestic brands are eligible for higher levels of support if they meet conditions regarding ownership structure, operational control, and intellectual property rights, while also establishing design and research centers within the country. Thus, the level of support depends not only on size and revenue growth but also on the extent of participation in the domestic supply chain, as well as design and R&D activities.
You may also like
To implement the MPMS, India has allocated 62,500 crore rupees, equivalent to approximately US$7.5 billion. The program spans five fiscal years, from 2026-2027 to 2030-2031, with grants determined based on business performance.
The design of the MPMS shows that India is not simply allocating resources to increase mobile phone production. By linking support levels to business results and specific business activities, the program simultaneously aims at three goals: expanding revenue, increasing the use of domestically sourced components, and bringing more design and R&D activities into India.
This also marks a shift after the PLI phase. While the previous phase contributed to the rapid expansion of smartphone production and exports, MPMS places greater emphasis on value creation and retention within the economy , through domestic supply chains and higher-tech activities.
What are the implications for Vietnam?
India's approach to linking support resources to business performance is particularly noteworthy in the context of increasing competition for investment among Asian economies, while Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies in line with Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy.
In a recent report, the Foreign Investment Agency of the Ministry of Finance noted that regional economies such as India, Malaysia , and Thailand are stepping up incentive packages to attract shifting capital flows, especially in strategic sectors like semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and renewable energy. This creates additional competitive pressure on Vietnam in attracting and retaining high-quality investment projects.
At the same time, the need to innovate the methods of investment incentives and support has been raised. Resolution 10 emphasizes the need to "gradually shift from traditional incentives to a support mechanism linked to the operational efficiency of projects."
You may also like
One of the tools Vietnam is using is the Investment Support Fund, established under Decree No. 182/2024/ND-CP. The fund aims to stabilize the investment environment; encourage and attract strategic investors and multinational corporations; and support domestic businesses in certain sectors requiring investment incentives. Businesses meeting the eligibility criteria can receive support for costs such as training, R&D, fixed asset investment, and the production of high-tech products.
The Investment Support Fund is designed for multiple sectors, rather than focusing on a specific industry like the MPMS. This difference highlights a noteworthy aspect of resource allocation. With the MPMS, India selects a specific industry, clearly defining desired outcomes, from revenue growth and domestic supply chain development to bringing design and R&D activities domestically, and then links support levels to each of those outcomes.
In the context of limited support resources and increasingly fierce competition for investment, the selection of priority sectors and the level of resource concentration have become crucial factors in policy design and implementation. Focusing more on a few industries and sectors with the potential to create high added value, form supply chains, and disseminate technology can help support resources have a more significant impact, rather than allocating them too broadly.
Besides leveraging the effectiveness of the Investment Support Fund under Decree 182 to retain investors and supply chains, in the face of fierce competition to attract investment, India's method of quantifying results to determine the level of support in the MPMS program provides valuable experience for Vietnam as it gradually shifts from traditional incentives to performance-based support mechanisms in the future.

articles.title: Week 42: Mexico Trade & Investment Highlights - Mexico Business News
articles.summary: Week 42: Mexico Trade & Investment Highlights  Mexico Business News
articles.full_text:
Summary: Mexico’s trade and investment strategy is increasingly focused on converting foreign capital, industrial expansion and infrastructure spending into higher-value domestic economic activity. Taiwanese companies employ approximately 75,000 people across 300 facilities in Mexico, while Nuevo Leon added 66,438 formal jobs through September 2026 and Queretaro identified MX$24.6 billion in potential investments; meanwhile, Mexico plans US$454 billion in infrastructure investment through 2030. Capturing greater value from these developments will depend on technology transfer, workforce development, stronger domestic suppliers, infrastructure execution and regulatory certainty.
Taiwanese companies employ approximately 75,000 people in Mexico and operate around 300 facilities, as bilateral trade reached a record US$48.2 billion in 2025, making Taiwan Mexico’s third-largest trading partner. Growing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing is creating opportunities to deepen industrial cooperation, expand supplier networks and strengthen Mexico’s participation in North American technology supply chains. Realizing greater economic value will depend on workforce training, technology transfer and the development of local capabilities in engineering, automation, testing and higher-value electronics production.
Nuevo Leon generated 66,438 formal jobs between January and September 2026, accounting for 16.2% of Mexico’s total new formal employment and bringing the state’s IMSS-registered workforce to a record 2 million workers. Manufacturing investment, including LEGO Group’s planned US$400 million expansion in Cienega de Flores, is supporting employment growth and creating opportunities for Mexican suppliers, particularly in plastics, chemicals and industrial inputs, as the state seeks to strengthen domestic supply chains and regional competitiveness.
Queretaro has identified 40 potential investment projects valued at more than MX$24.6 billion, with the potential to generate 10,252 jobs, as the state seeks to attract capital and strengthen local business competitiveness. Complementing its investment pipeline, the state is supporting micro, small and medium-sized enterprises through certification, professionalization and supplier-development programs, while its expanding data center and advanced manufacturing sectors create additional opportunities for local companies to participate in AI infrastructure and North American supply chains.
CANACINTRA established its Mexico-Asia-Pacific Strategic Cooperation Commission on Oct. 8 to expand technology transfer, foreign investment and supply-chain integration, creating potential opportunities for Mexican manufacturers in advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, electromobility and green energy. In Queretaro, the initiative aligns with a pipeline of 40 prospective investment projects valued at more than MX$24.6 billion and potentially generating 10,252 jobs, although the economic impact will depend on securing concrete partnerships and strengthening local suppliers’ technical capabilities.
Mexico plans to invest MX$8.4 trillion (US$454 billion) in public and mixed-financing infrastructure projects through 2030, targeting energy, highways, ports, railways and water systems to strengthen logistics, industrial competitiveness and economic growth. President Claudia Sheinbaum’s strategy combines public spending, private capital and development banking, while business leaders emphasize fiscal discipline, investment-grade creditworthiness, domestic supply chain integration and regulatory certainty ahead of the USMCA review. The plan’s economic impact will depend on financing, project execution and its ability to address infrastructure bottlenecks while expanding opportunities for Mexican suppliers and small businesses.

articles.summary: New York’s Plaza Hotel to Close in 2027 for at Least Four Years  The Hollywood ReporterPlaza Hotel to Shut for Four-Year Cleanup of Its Celebrated Facade  The New York TimesPlaza Hotel closure leaves bride scrambling for new wedding venue  ABC7 New York6 luxury NYC hotels to visit while The Plaza Hotel is closed  NewsdayExclusive | Frustrated Plaza brides scrambling to save six-figure dream weddings after iconic hotel’s shocking closure  New York...
articles.full_text:
New York City’s historic Plaza Hotel will close its doors in January 2027 for at least four years as it undergoes extensive restoration work on its landmark-protected facade, according to its operator, Fairmont Hotels & Resorts. The hotel is expected to remain closed until 2031 if cleanup is completed on time, though a reopening date has not yet been announced.
The closure will affect the hotel’s 282 guest rooms, event spaces and Palm Court restaurant, which are also expected to close in January, according to The New York Times. The property also houses 181 condominium units, though it remains unclear whether the restoration will affect residents.
Fairmont Hotels & Resorts declined to comment.
Opened in 1907, the Plaza sits at the corner of Fifth Avenue and Central Park South, overlooking Central Park. Designed by architect Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, the 18-story building features French Renaissance-style architecture. The hotel was designated a New York City landmark in 1969.
The Plaza has also become a recognizable site in movies and television. Titles that were either shot or set in the hotel include Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992), in which Macaulay Culkin’s Kevin McCallister stays at the hotel, as well as North by Northwest (1959), The Way We Were (1973) and Eloise at the Plaza (2003), among others.
President Donald Trump also owned The Plaza from 1988 to 1995. Trump made a cameo in Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.
The upcoming closure marks another major interruption in the Plaza’s history. The hotel previously shut down in 2005 for a renovation that converted many of its original guest rooms into private residences before reopening in 2008.

articles.title: 74 Educational Products Analyzed: What Strategies Are Driving the Fastest-Growing Companies in the Industry? - 36Kr
articles.summary: 74 Educational Products Analyzed: What Strategies Are Driving the Fastest-Growing Companies in the Industry?  36Kr
articles.full_text:
We have taken stock of 74 educational products, what are the fastest-growing companies doing?
Recently, Feifan Industry Research released the global education product traffic ranking for September 2026 based on Similarweb statistics, covering categories including education, homework assistants, AI tutoring and language learning, with a total of 74 products included, and the total monthly visits reaching approximately 216 million.
Judging from the ranking, the global education product market presents three distinct characteristics.
First, traffic is highly concentrated. Quizlet and Duolingo firmly occupy the top two positions, together contributing over 60% of total visits, and mature learning platforms still hold a large market share.
Second, emerging AI products are growing rapidly. Among the 71 products with month-on-month data, 56 have achieved an increase in visits. Among them, Solvely, Astra AI and Class Companion all recorded a month-on-month increase of over 100% in both visits and unique visitors.
Third, AI education products are further penetrating into segmented scenarios. Learning notes, memory training and intelligent problem-solving have become the main application directions, and products with rapid growth have also emerged in fields such as teacher assistance, language learning and vocational skill training. In addition to leading US enterprises, Chinese overseas-oriented products and European start-ups have also secured a place in the global educational AI market.
Combining the traffic performance in September, as well as financing, product updates and business layouts since 2026, Duojing has sorted out several most noteworthy edtech companies.
 Quizlet: Acquired AI note-taking company to expand one-stop learning services
In September, US online learning platform Quizlet topped the list with approximately 71.95 million monthly visits, representing a month-on-month increase of 70.79%.
Founded in 2005, Quizlet initially started with digital flashcards and memory training, and is currently accelerating its transformation into a comprehensive AI learning platform. In February this year, the company acquired Coconote, an AI note-taking application that can convert class recordings and videos into learning materials such as notes, flashcards and quizzes. Coconote is a wildly popular AI note-taking tool among overseas students, with total content views exceeding 1 billion across all platforms in the 18 months before the acquisition, and it is deeply loved by college students. Its core capability is to automatically organize class recordings and online course videos into structured notes, flashcards, quiz questions and learning podcasts.
Meanwhile, Quizlet launched an AI conversational learning function, which supports students to get explanations by asking questions and generate practice content.
After that, Quizlet continued to expand external cooperation. In March, the company officially integrated ChatGPT, allowing users to generate learning flashcards during conversations; in June, it launched the Google Classroom plug-in to help teachers assign learning tasks and track students' completion status.
Through acquisition and product integration, Quizlet is extending its original knowledge memory services to links such as class recording, learning material generation and teaching management, expanding its coverage in students' autonomous learning and school teaching scenarios.
 Solvely: Expanding from AI problem-solving to vocational qualification examination training
Solvely, which started with photo-based problem-solving, is extending its business to a wider range of learning and vocational training scenarios.
In April this year, Solvely announced that it was selected into the first Prosumer AI 40 list jointly launched by Notable Capital and Nasdaq. The company disclosed at the same time that its platform has covered more than 150 countries and regions. In addition to AI problem-solving, it also provides functions such as learning notes, flashcards and mock exams, and has extended its services to vocational qualification examination fields including the US nurse license exam, nursing school entrance exam and commercial driving license exam.
This expansion is also accompanied by traffic growth. In September, Solvely recorded approximately 1.93 million monthly visits, with a month-on-month increase of 246.04%, ranking first in the growth rate of this education product ranking.
On October 10, Solvely further disclosed its technical layout of educational AI agents. Through models optimized for educational tasks, combined with step-by-step explanations, interactive visualization and practice tools, it helps students understand knowledge. Its product positioning is extending from a single problem-solving tool to a comprehensive AI learning platform.
 Astra AI: Building a global AI tutor platform without external financing
Astra AI, an edtech company from Slovenia, is expanding the global market through subscription-based AI tutoring services.
Co-founded by Andrej P. Škraba and Klemen Selakovič, Astra AI initially focused on math tutoring and now covers multiple subjects including physics, chemistry and languages. Students can upload notes, courseware and past exam papers, and the AI will generate personalized learning plans, and complete review through course explanations, flashcards, quizzes and other methods.
This year, the founders of Astra AI publicly disclosed that the company's total registered users have exceeded 10 million, with annual recurring revenue (ARR) reaching 25 million US dollars, representing a roughly 25-fold increase over the past year. It is particularly noteworthy that the company stated that its business growth mainly relies on its own operating income and has not introduced venture capital.
This growth is also reflected in the September ranking. Astra AI reached 5.242 million monthly visits, with a month-on-month increase of 204.75%, ranking 7th on the list. Compared with educational AI startups that rely on financing to expand their scale, Astra AI provides another development sample: supporting product R&D with subscription revenue and expanding to overseas markets through multilingual localization.
 Gizmo: Completed a new round of financing to step up gamified AI learning
In April this year, British AI learning platform Gizmo announced the completion of a 22 million US dollars Series A financing round, led by Shine Capital, with participation from institutions including Ada Ventures, GSV and NFX. At the time of financing, the company's total users had exceeded 13 million, covering more than 120 countries, while its team only had 7 employees at that time.
Founded in 2021 by three University of Cambridge graduates, Gizmo focuses on gamified learning. After students upload notes, documents or web links, the AI can automatically generate learning materials such as flashcards and interactive quizzes, and improve learning engagement through mechanisms such as consecutive learning rewards, leaderboards and friend challenges.
This model also brings rapid user growth. In 2023, Gizmo had approximately 300,000 cumulative users, which had exceeded 13 million by April this year. In September, Gizmo ranked 3rd in the education product ranking with approximately 7.85 million monthly visits, with a month-on-month increase of 73.28%.
After the new round of financing, Gizmo plans to expand its AI and engineering teams, focus on expanding the US college student market, and continuously improve its learning products. The development path of this company also provides a case for how AI education products can acquire and retain users through gamified design.
 Gauth: Moving from AI problem-solving to AI course generation
Gauth, an overseas education app under ByteDance, began to shift its business focus from photo-based problem-solving to AI courses this year.
On September 1, Gauth announced the full launch of AI Course, adding more than 200 new math courses covering content such as US high school algebra, geometry and AP Calculus. Different from traditional pre-recorded courses, Gauth uses AI to generate course explanations, visual content and quizzes. Students can also independently input learning topics to generate courses that meet their personal needs and share them with other users.
While launching new features, Gauth continued to maintain growth. According to Similarweb data, its monthly visits in September were approximately 4.7 million, with a month-on-month increase of 40.88%, ranking 9th in the education product ranking. The company disclosed at the same time that since its launch in 2020, Gauth's total global downloads have exceeded 200 million.
In October, Gauth further launched the "Infinite Digital Canvas" feature, allowing students and AI tutors to explain, write and solve problems on the same interactive whiteboard, reducing the fragmentation between traditional video courses and chat-based Q&A.
From providing answers to questions to generating complete courses, and then to interactive teaching, Gauth is trying to apply AI to course content production and personalized teaching to further expand the overseas education market.
 Class Companion: AI grading tool integrated into school teaching management system
In the September education product ranking, Class Companion is one of the fastest-growing teacher-side AI products. Its monthly visits increased by 136.76% month-on-month, and monthly unique visitors increased by 119.56% month-on-month. Both growth rates ranked top 3 among the 74 products, outperforming similar platforms such as MagicSchool AI.
Class Companion is an AI teaching tool for K12 schools in the US, mainly helping teachers grade essays, provide personalized feedback, and analyze students' knowledge mastery. articles.title: China's 15th Five-Year Financial Agenda: Dinpay Global Steps Up Cross-border Payment Push to Advance - openPR.com
articles.summary: China's 15th Five-Year Financial Agenda: Dinpay Global Steps Up Cross-border Payment Push to Advance  openPR.com
articles.full_text:
The central-bank document envisions a multi-tier, wide-reaching RMB cross-border payment system and better-connected cross-border financial infrastructure. It also stresses risk mitigation alongside market opening. Industry observers note the framework creates fresh opportunities for domestic cross-border payment providers to support real-economy outbound expansion.
Dinpay Global is the upgraded global business division of Dinpay, one of China's leading payment companies. Focusing on high-growth outbound sectors such as cross-border e-commerce, international air travel, cross-border logistics and overseas trade in services, the platform delivers a full suite of cross-border financial solutions including RMB settlement, global account management, foreign exchange purchase-and-payment, and currency conversion.
Small and medium-sized Chinese exporters have long grappled with clunky settlement workflows, high forex expenses and sluggish capital turnover. Dinpay Global connects domestic payment rails with overseas local clearing networks to build a streamlined multi-channel cross-border capital transfer framework. It has sealed a strategic cooperation with Jiangsu Electronic Port to roll out a digital trade solution enabling "payment upon customs declaration". Direct system integration removes manual data entry and paper-based formalities, shortens processing cycles and cuts overall operating costs for trading enterprises.
Via standardized API integrations, businesses can connect lightweightly to Dinpay Global and rapidly set up global inbound-outbound payment flows. The platform accommodates diverse, fragmented transaction types ranging from traditional foreign trade and high-frequency cross-border e-commerce payments to goods and service-trade settlements, meeting full-lifecycle capital needs for firms going global, aligning with the policy goal of wide service coverage.
For all business expansion, compliance and risk management remain top priorities for cross-border finance. Dinpay Global embeds risk controls across its entire operation and adheres strictly to domestic regulatory requirements. It maintains robust transaction monitoring and compliance screening systems, supported by rigorous customer identity verification, segregated client fund management and complete transaction record-keeping, forming safeguards for cross-border RMB circulation.
Looking ahead, the cross-border payment sector is poised for growth amid advancing RMB internationalization throughout the 15th Five-Year period. Dinpay Global states it will keep aligning with central-bank reforms, upgrade its RMB-denominated cross-border offerings and explore new use-cases. It aims to underpin China's high-level financial opening-up through secure, efficient and inclusive cross-border payment capabilities.

articles.full_text:
CAIRO, Oct 16 (MENA) - Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met on Friday with Daechapon Lersuwanaroj, Executive Director of Thailand’s Export-Import Bank, during his visit to Bangkok, to discuss strengthening financing support for bilateral trade and joint investments.
During the meeting, Abdelatty stressed the importance of leveraging the bank’s financing, insurance and investment guarantee instruments to encourage Thai companies to expand their operations in Egypt.
He outlined Egypt’s advantages as a regional manufacturing and export hub, highlighting investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone and access to African, Arab and European markets through free trade agreements.
The talks also covered expanding credit facilities and facilitating payments to support exporters and importers in both countries. (MENA)

articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Electronic Equipment And Instruments market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global market for Electronic Equipment and Instruments is a cornerstone of modern industrial and technological infrastructure, encompassing test and measurement devices, analytical instruments, signal generators, oscilloscopes, data acquisition systems, and navigation apparatus. As of 2026, the market is valued at approximately $XX billion and is projected to expand at a CAGR of 5.2% from 2026 to 2035, reaching $XX billion by 2035. This growth is underpinned by accelerating industrial automation, the global rollout of 5G networks, rising R&D expenditure in electronics and pharmaceuticals, and increasing demand for precision testing in aerospace and defense.
The market is characterized by high R&D intensity, rapid technological cycles, and a competitive landscape where software integration and data analytics are becoming key differentiators. While supply chain disruptions and trade tensions pose risks, the long-term outlook remains positive, with emerging applications in IoT, electric vehicles, and environmental monitoring creating new demand streams. This report provides a data-driven analysis of market size, segmentation, end-use sectors, regional dynamics, and competitive strategies, offering stakeholders a transparent view of the path to 2035.
The baseline scenario for the Electronic Equipment and Instruments market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates steady expansion, with global market value rising at a compound annual growth rate of 5.2%. This outlook assumes no major global recessions, a gradual easing of semiconductor supply constraints, and continued investment in digital infrastructure. Demand will be strongest in Asia-Pacific, particularly China and India, where manufacturing upgrades and 5G deployment are accelerating. North America and Europe will see moderate growth, driven by defense modernization, automotive electrification, and healthcare R&D.
Key product segments such as data acquisition systems and spectrum analyzers are expected to outpace the overall market due to their critical role in 5G, IoT, and autonomous systems. However, pricing pressure in mature segments like multimeters and oscilloscopes will persist, offset by value-added software and services. The market index is projected to reach 152 by 2035 (2025=100), reflecting a 52% increase over the decade. Risks include geopolitical trade barriers, component shortages, and slower-than-expected adoption of Industry 4.0 in some regions.
Nevertheless, the fundamental demand drivers remain robust, and the market is poised for sustained growth, with opportunities in calibration services, portable instruments, and AI-enabled analytics.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Accelerating industrial automation and Industry 4.0 adoption, requiring advanced sensors, controllers, and test equipment for smart factories.
- Global 5G network deployment and expansion, driving demand for spectrum analyzers, signal generators, and network testing instruments.
- Rising R&D expenditure in electronics, pharmaceuticals, and automotive sectors, fueling demand for analytical and test instruments.
- Increasing defense and aerospace budgets worldwide, necessitating precision navigation, radar, and electronic warfare testing equipment.
- Growth in electric vehicle production and autonomous driving technology, requiring specialized automotive testing and calibration instruments.
- Expansion of IoT and connected devices, creating demand for data acquisition systems and wireless test solutions.
Potential Growth Constraints
- Ongoing global semiconductor shortage and supply chain disruptions, delaying instrument production and increasing costs.
- Geopolitical trade tensions and export controls, particularly between the US and China, restricting market access and technology transfer.
- High initial cost of advanced instruments, limiting adoption among small and medium-sized enterprises.
- Rapid technological obsolescence, requiring continuous R&D investment and shortening product lifecycles.
- Shortage of skilled personnel for operating and maintaining sophisticated test and measurement equipment.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Industrial Automation and Control (estimated share: 28%)
Industrial automation and control represents the largest end-use sector for electronic equipment and instruments, accounting for approximately 28% of global demand in 2026. This segment encompasses programmable logic controllers, sensors, data acquisition systems, and calibration equipment used in manufacturing plants, process industries, and utilities. The current demand is driven by the need to improve operational efficiency, reduce downtime, and ensure product quality. Through 2035, the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies, including cyber-physical systems and digital twins, will accelerate, requiring more sophisticated measurement and control instruments.
Demand-side indicators to watch include manufacturing PMI, industrial robot installations, and investment in smart factory initiatives. The shift toward predictive maintenance and real-time analytics will boost demand for wireless sensors and edge computing devices. Major companies in this space include Siemens, Rockwell Automation, Honeywell, and Emerson Electric, which are integrating AI and cloud connectivity into their instrument offerings. Current trend: Growing at a robust pace due to smart manufacturing and IIoT adoption..

Representative participants: Siemens, Rockwell Automation, Honeywell, Emerson Electric, ABB, and Schneider Electric.
Research and Development Labs (estimated share: 22%)
Research and development labs are a critical end-use sector, accounting for about 22% of the market. These labs, spanning academia, government, and corporate R&D, rely on oscilloscopes, spectrum analyzers, signal generators, and analytical instruments for prototyping, testing, and validation. Current demand is fueled by breakthroughs in semiconductors, quantum computing, and biotechnology. Over the forecast period to 2035, R&D expenditure is expected to rise, particularly in Asia-Pacific and North America, driven by government initiatives and private sector innovation. Key demand indicators include R&D spending as a percentage of GDP, number of patents filed, and venture capital investment in deep tech.
The trend toward miniaturization and higher frequencies in electronics will require instruments with greater precision and bandwidth. Companies like Keysight, Tektronix (Fortive), and National Instruments are key suppliers, focusing on software-defined instruments and modular platforms. Major trends: Rising R&D budgets in semiconductor and quantum technologies, Shift toward software-defined and modular instruments, Increasing demand for high-frequency and high-bandwidth test equipment, Growth in life sciences research driving analytical instrument demand, and Adoption of cloud-based data management in labs.
Representative participants: Keysight Technologies, Fortive (Tektronix), National Instruments, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bruker, and Shimadzu.
Telecommunications (estimated share: 18%)
Telecommunications is a key end-use sector, representing around 18% of the market. Instruments such as spectrum analyzers, vector network analyzers, and signal generators are essential for deploying, testing, and maintaining wireless and wireline networks. The ongoing global 5G rollout is the primary demand driver, requiring testing at sub-6 GHz and mmWave frequencies. Through 2035, the evolution to 5G-Advanced and 6G research will sustain demand for advanced test equipment. Demand-side indicators include telecom capital expenditure, number of 5G base stations deployed, and data traffic growth.
The increasing complexity of networks, including network slicing and edge computing, will necessitate sophisticated monitoring and optimization tools. Major players like Anritsu, Rohde & Schwarz, and Keysight are at the forefront, offering solutions for 5G NR, O-RAN, and fiber testing. Representative participants: Anritsu, Rohde & Schwarz, Keysight Technologies, VIAVI Solutions, EXFO, and Spirent Communications.
Aerospace and Defense (estimated share: 17%)
Aerospace and defense accounts for approximately 17% of the market, with demand for navigation, radar, electronic warfare, and communication testing instruments. These instruments must meet stringent reliability and precision standards. Current demand is driven by increased defense budgets in the US, China, and NATO countries, as well as growing commercial space activity. Over the forecast period, modernization programs, hypersonic weapons development, and satellite constellations will fuel demand for advanced RF and microwave test equipment.
