articles.title: Opinion: China’s export boom has a hidden bill; Asean is already paying - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: Opinion: China’s export boom has a hidden bill; Asean is already paying  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
For a decade, Southeast Asia has sold a rather attractive story about the US–China rift: let the giants throw furniture at each other; we will take the factory bookings.
Production relocates. Supply chains diversify. Investors arrive with spreadsheets, site plans and an urgent need for somewhere else to build. Whatever happens between Washington and Beijing, someone still has to make the goods. Asean has land, workers and a ribbon-cutting ceremony ready to go.
It is a compelling pitch. It also assumes that another factory means another opportunity. In a market already swimming in goods, another factory can mean another casualty.
Michael Froman, president of the Council on Foreign Relations, argues in Foreign Affairs that China has grown too large to keep exporting its way around weak demand at home. The next global economic crisis, he warns, could be made in China.
Read that from Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta or Bangkok, and the warning lands rather closer to the kitchen table.
Asean is exposed twice over. Chinese overcapacity undercuts the region’s producers. Meanwhile, the region depends heavily on Chinese demand, which rests on households that are not spending enough. Southeast Asia needs China’s customers to open their wallets while its manufacturers try to survive the output of China’s factories.
These risks are often presented as a tidy sequence: first comes the flood of goods; later, if China’s economic model buckles, comes the slowdown.
Economics has declined to respect the running order. Weak demand at home is a large part of why China exports so aggressively in the first place. Both pressures are already here, sharing the same front door. A Chinese crisis would turn up the volume on both.
Consider the machinery behind the flood.
China’s trade surplus approached US$1.2 trillion (RM4.9 trillion) in 2025, according to Froman’s figures, while nearly 30% of its industrial firms were losing money. Elsewhere, losses on that scale would eventually force capacity out of the market. In China, local governments protect jobs, banks roll over weak loans, and firms slash prices to hang on to market share.
The factory keeps running. The losses keep accumulating. The goods keep looking for somewhere to go.
The OECD’s industrial subsidies database offers a sense of the financial scaffolding holding this up. Across its sample of 525 of the world’s largest industrial firms, Chinese companies received between three and eight times the government support of OECD-based competitors from 2005 to 2024. The OECD links almost 60% of those Chinese firms’ global market-share gains to that support.
This is a sample, not a census, and the OECD calls its estimate conservative. Those qualifications matter. So does the uncomfortable conclusion: Asean manufacturers are competing against rivals backed by a financing system willing to tolerate losses.
Try explaining that to a factory owner whose bank expects the loan repaid on schedule.
The sheer scale of the capacity makes the problem harder to shrug off. Froman puts China’s annual solar manufacturing capacity at about 1,200 gigawatts, roughly twice the previous year’s global installations. Its capacity for electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids stands at about 25 million units, against domestic demand of 12 million.
Capacity is not output. An available production line does not automatically become a finished car. But it creates relentless pressure to find buyers, cut prices or swallow losses. When the machinery is there, the jobs depend on it and the financing keeps coming, switching it off becomes a remarkably unpopular suggestion.
Much of the resulting pressure washes up in Southeast Asia.
The European Central Bank found that Chinese export volumes to Asean rose sharply in 2025 while unit prices fell in most sectors. More goods, cheaper prices: a cheerful combination for the purchasing department, a rather less cheerful one for the factory down the road.
A September 2025 Bank of Thailand study found that Thai imports from China had nearly doubled over a decade, compared with roughly 20% growth in imports from everywhere else. It counted more than 200,000 Thai small- and medium-sized enterprises, employing over two million workers, making goods that compete with those imports.
That is a measure of exposure, not a tally of closures. It should not be dressed up as one. But two million workers is a large number of livelihoods to leave sitting beneath an increasingly heavy cloud.
Then there is e-commerce, which gives the flood another entrance. Goods can reach consumers while bypassing local retailers altogether. The competition now arrives on the phone screen, complete with a checkout button.
Governments have responded with different tools. Malaysia’s 2024 sales tax on low-value imports was largely an exercise in fairness, closing a tax gap that allowed overseas online sellers to undercut local ones. Thailand followed with VAT in July 2024. Indonesia’s 2024 threat of tariffs of up to 200% on some Chinese goods came with a more openly protective message.
And for anyone tempted to prescribe the usual cure, “move up the value chain”, Germany offers a sobering exhibit.
Froman reports that German car exports to China fell by two-thirds from their 2022 peak by 2025, while China’s own vehicle exports more than doubled. The old development ladder assumed that poorer countries would inherit industries as richer ones moved on to more sophisticated work.
That ladder becomes considerably less useful when the world’s largest manufacturer is competing on every rung.
Cheap Chinese inputs still help many Asean firms become more competitive. That benefit is real, and governments should count it. But the very same bargain can be an existential threat to the local company making the product.
One firm’s cheaper input is another firm’s disappearing order book. Policy has to read both sets of accounts.
The demand side of the relationship brings its own complications.
Weak Chinese consumption does not automatically mean falling Chinese demand for Asean goods. China can underconsume while importing more chips, ores and other industrial inputs. Asean–China trade continued to grow in 2025.
Yet China’s imports rose just 0.5% in yuan terms last year, against 6.1% growth in exports. The outward conveyor belt was moving considerably faster than the inward one. And Southeast Asia’s dependence on Chinese final demand runs deeper than direct export figures suggest.
The IMF’s 2025 assessment of Malaysia estimates that about 8% of the country’s domestic value added was ultimately absorbed by Chinese final demand in 2022. That is an exposure measure, not a forecast of losses. It nevertheless shows how much Malaysian economic activity ultimately depends on a customer in China, even when the route between the two is less than obvious.
A 2016 IMF study found that every percentage point shaved off Chinese growth could reduce growth in the five largest Asean economies by between 0.2 and 0.5 percentage points. The estimates are dated. The channels through which the damage travels remain very much in business.
Commodities. Components. Tourism. Investment.
Froman recalls China’s investment slowdown between 2012 and 2015, when copper, oil and iron ore prices fell hard. For economies selling into China’s appetite for construction and industry, a change in that appetite can quickly become a problem at home.
Alongside the pressures from goods and demand sits a third channel: finance.
An IMF–World Bank assessment in February placed Laos in debt distress. Chinese lenders were its largest creditors, and Chinese debt-service deferrals were providing relief. If a crisis at home forced Beijing to pull back overseas lending, sustaining that flexibility could become harder.
The creditor with room to accommodate you today may have its own cash-flow meeting tomorrow.
Put these channels together and a Chinese downturn offers Asean little prospect of a breather. The region could face more discounted goods, fewer export orders, weaker commodity prices and tighter credit, all arriving together.
A clearance sale outside the factory gate is scant comfort when customers are cancelling orders and the bank is becoming less accommodating.
Nor does moving a factory into Asean provide an automatic escape route from the trade war. A new address is useful. It is not a geopolitical invisibility cloak.
In April 2025, the US Commerce Department made final anti-dumping and countervailing duty findings against solar cells from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam. It ruled that firms operating there had received Chinese government subsidies, in one of Washington’s first findings of transnational subsidies.
The factory had crossed a border. The subsidy question had followed it.
That case was a preview. A July 2025 US order added a 40% tariff on goods found to have been transshipped to evade duties. Chinese inputs or Chinese ownership alone did not establish evasion, an important distinction that should survive the political shouting.
The measure fell with the Supreme Court’s February 2026 ruling against emergency-powers tariffs. Washington’s broader direction, however, has not changed.
In March, it opened Section 301 investigations into “structural excess capacity” in 16 economies, including six Asean members. Since July 24, separate duties have added 10% on covered goods from Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia.
Washington increasingly sees parts of Southeast Asia as belonging inside the overcapacity problem. The region’s carefully marketed refuge now appears on the inspection list.
Malaysia has already tightened its origin rules to require at least 25% local content. Investment that contributes little beyond final assembly now attracts scrutiny in precisely the markets it was supposed to unlock.
Meanwhile, Asean is drawing closer to China. The upgraded Asean–China Free Trade Area, signed in Kuala Lumpur last October, extends into the digital and green economies and su

articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry (Miti) will continue to expand and strengthen Malaysia's export markets through initiatives under the 2027 Budget.
Deputy Minister Sim Tze Tzin said Miti, through the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation, would lead export-strengthening initiatives through the RM60 million Export Capacity Building Programme and the RM50 million Export Strengthening and Market Diversification Fund.
The initiatives would also be supported by RM1 billion in financing facilities from Bank Pembangunan Malaysia Bhd and RM10 million through EXIM Bank.
"Through 200 export promotion activities, the programme is expected to directly benefit more than 3,500 local companies, with export sales targeted to reach RM12 billion by the end of 2027," he said in a statement.
The deputy minister said efforts to facilitate business would also be intensified through collaboration between the Malaysia Productivity Corporation and the Special Task Force on Agency Reform to reduce bureaucratic red tape.
He revealed that the regulatory reform initiative had so far helped save industries RM3.71 billion in compliance costs and expedite business licence approvals.
Sim said Miti is also focusing on developing viable regional industrial clusters to promote balanced economic growth nationwide. The comprehensive and integrated implementation of these initiatives was expected to enhance Malaysia's standing as a leading regional investment destination and a sustainable global trade hub.
"These efforts include the ministry's strategic initiatives to drive the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, develop automotive and maritime hubs in Perak, and strengthen the semiconductor chip technology ecosystem in Penang and Kedah," he added.
"They also involve expanding trade corridor infrastructure in Perlis and developing a planning framework for a Special Economic Zone in Sibu, Sarawak."

articles.title: The State of the Australian Investor 2026 - Morningstar Australia
articles.summary: The State of the Australian Investor 2026  Morningstar Australia
articles.full_text:
Data on how Australian retail investors think and act.
Mentioned: Vanguard Australian Shares ETF (VAS), BetaShares NASDAQ 100 ETF (NDQ), Vanguard MSCI Intl ETF (VGS), Perth Mint Gold Structured Product (PMGOLD), Betashares Global Shares ETF (BGBL), Global X Physical Gold Structured (GOLD), iShares S&P 500 ETF (IVV), Global X Semiconductor ETF (SEMI), Vanguard Australian Shares High Yld ETF (VHY), CSL Ltd (CSL), BHP Group Ltd (BHP), Woodside Energy Group Ltd (WDS), The a2 Milk Co Ltd (A2M), Fortescue Ltd (FMG), Mineral Resources Ltd (MIN), Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA)
Executive Summary
The 2026 State of the Australian Investor report marries qualitative survey data from the largely self-direct and engaged retail investors within the Morningstar community with quantitative portfolio, performance and transaction data from an overlapping and expanded group of retail investors using Sharesight for portfolio tracking and management. This unique view of Australian retail investors shows both the mindset and behaviour of this population.
You can find the PDF version of the report here.
Report key findings
- Investors are cautious, but remain pragmatic and continue to take advantage of perceived opportunities.
- A structural shift in retail portfolios continues with Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) becoming the core building blocks of investor portfolios while individual shares are transitioning to satellite holdings.
- Retail investors have generated strong average returns but behaviour influences results with investors who trade more frequently earning lower median returns.
- Income remains a priority for individual investors with recent changes to capital gains tax likely increasing the appeal of income strategies.
- Home bias is persistent in Australian portfolios but there is evidence to suggest its prevalence may be overstated given the limited data on the asset allocation of ETFs which are increasingly used to gain global exposure.
The Australian investor of 2026 is best described not as bullish or bearish, but as cautious and engaged. The Morningstar community is concerned about geopolitics, inflation, economic recessions, the cost of living, market volatility and changes to the tax environment. A significant portion of these investors classify themselves as cautious.
Yet these concerns don’t translate into a broad retreat from markets. During the major market shocks from the last several years, retail investors continued to take advantage of perceived opportunities and were net buyers during market shocks. On the busiest trading day of each of the three shocks examined, buys exceeded sells by roughly two to one.
This gap between sentiment and action indicates the pragmatic long-term approach of many investors, which is likely influenced by the continued resilience of equity markets since the pandemic. Investors have been conditioned to see market drops as temporary opportunities to take advantage of lower prices. They continue to ‘buy the dip.’
A structural shift continues in the way investors access markets with ETFs becoming the default building block of the retail portfolio. While strong fund flows into ETFs is widely reported the extent of this structural change in markets may be masked by data on overall portfolio holdings.
Direct shares still represent 51.50% of overall portfolios but it is likely that this is influenced by legacy positions. New investors allocate a higher percentage of their portfolio to ETFs at 40% compared to 26.20% for the overall population. Across the entire population of portfolios the four most widely held securities are all ETFs and transaction data shows ETFs dominate ongoing retail investor purchases.
The emerging retail portfolio looks to be hybrid: diversified ETFs form the core, while individual companies are used to express conviction. The buy-to-sell ratios reinforce this interpretation. ETF purchases outnumbered ETF sales by 3.2 - 5.4 times, varying by quarter. For individual shares, the ratio remained tightly clustered between 1.5 and 1.7 times. ETFs look increasingly like accumulate-and-hold positions; individual stocks are where investors are more willing to revise views based on market conditions.
The changing nature of investor portfolios is influenced by the market environment. Strong overall returns have been driven by the largest companies and market capitalisation indexes have become increasingly top- heavy. This market environment is dovetailing with persistent evidence that active stock pickers struggle to beat the market.
In response, retail investors are turning to passively managed ETFs. Established investors are steadily shifting their portfolios to a core/satellite approach. New investors without legacy positions and significant unrealised capital gains begin with core ETF holdings and build their satellite.
Many investors are shifting to global markets which have outperformed the Australian market since the global financial crisis. ETFs are the vehicle of choice for many retail investors to gain global exposure. This global shift is evident in the strong average returns retail investors have enjoyed over the past two financial years which far surpassed the local market.
However, the average returns were not enjoyed by all investors. Investor behaviour played a large role with returns consistently falling as investors traded more.
Finally, retail investors are focusing on the income component of total returns. The proportion of total returns stemming from income indicates that investors are intentionally seeking income-producing investments. This is likely reflective of several concerns voiced by the Morningstar community including the impact of tax and the overall geopolitical environment.
What this report measures
What does the Australian investor look like today?
Investors are navigating a complex environment. Higher living costs, changing interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty, tax and superannuation policy changes and an increasingly complex investment landscape. At the same time, the return environment has been strong, with the investment product industry providing cheap and effective exposure to an increasingly diverse set of asset classes. Investors have access to more information than ever before.
This report looks to explore how retail investors in Australia are responding to this complex landscape. The State of the Australian Investor brings together four different sets of insights to provide a holistic view of the Australian investor:
The State of the Australian Investor provides a unique view of Australian investors by following the path from intention to action by using these four sets of insights.
An example of the interplay between intention and action is how investors react to market corrections. Survey data indicates investors are cautious but 93% would either hold or buy during a correction of 10% or more. During volatile markets content consumption rises as investors seek information to understand market movements. Investors are not just seeking information but also acting. Transaction data from Sharesight shows trading levels increasing during these periods. On days with increased volatility, investors are taking advantage of perceived opportunities as buys exceed sells by roughly two to one.
This sequence tells us substantially more than any individual statistic. It suggests that caution is not equivalent to paralysis and despite a measured outlook investors are not capitulating during meaningful selloffs. Investors can feel uncertain, consume more information and still conclude that the appropriate action is to maintain or increase exposure.
Who is the Australian investor?
The Morningstar community is an experienced and financially engaged cohort of investors. Around 65% of respondents had been investing for more than 20 years, while only around 5% had been investing for three years or less. Around 69% reported at least $1 million invested, excluding the home and including superannuation. About 63% said they make their investment decisions completely themselves, with another 21% making most decisions themselves.
The report is not principally describing a novice investor discovering markets for the first time. It reflects the views of people with substantial exposure to financial markets and a high degree of self-direction.
The Sharesight data broadly reinforces this picture as their cohort of retail investors are actively engaged in tracking their portfolios.
The sample may not be representative of the broader Australian investing population but indicates how engaged investors view and manage their portfolios. A growing number of Australians meet this criteria. In the latest ASX Investor Study, the number of Australian investors holding investments outside of a house and superannuation grew from 9 million in 2020 to 10.2 million in 2023. That is equivalent to more than half of the Australian adult population. In addition, 22% of on-exchange investors had started investing in the previous two years.
There is also an important distinction between engagement and activity. The median investor made only five trades in FY2026. The distribution of trading activity is highly skewed: a relatively small active group accounts for a disproportionate share of transactions.
One driver of the low median number of annual trades may be knowledge and engagement. There is significant evidence that over-trading leads to poor outcomes which is frequently cited in Morningstar content. This is also consistent with surveyed investors view of themselves. When asked, the Morningstar community believes that they have the knowledge and temperament to make good decisions self-ranking themselves at 73 out of 100.
This view is also consistent with faith in retirement outcomes with 78% of investors confident they have enough for retirement and 94% knowing exactly or roughly how much income they will need in retirement.

articles.title: Where are we in the power equipment industry cycle? - 36Kr
articles.summary: Where are we in the power equipment industry cycle?  36Kr
articles.full_text:
Over the past year or more, electrical equipment has been one of the most volatile sectors on the A-share market (the electrical equipment here includes both main grid equipment, and power electronics and power supply links). A number of companies quickly became double-bagger stocks first, then took a sharp downturn after May 2026, with most of their market value cut by half from the highs.
During the same period when the A-share market cooled down from a hot state, leading companies such as Siyuan Electric and Eagle Energy successively disclosed their prospectuses on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, planning to raise additional financing. The market is cooling down while capital activities are heating up. This seemingly contradictory combination just provides the best perspective to inspect the quality of this round of electrical equipment sector.
Return to the Starting Point After Frenzy
First, let's make a simple review of the market trend.
Essentially, this round of electrical equipment market rally is the result of the resonance of three main lines: grid equipment going global, large-scale energy storage overseas, and AI power supply chain. The three main lines continued to gain momentum from 2025 to 2026, pushing almost all sub-segments including transformers, tap changers, energy storage systems, AI power supplies, HVDC/SST into the fast track of valuation expansion.
The continuous decline since May 2026 does not mean that the above fundamental logic has suddenly collapsed, but that "the narrative has changed". On the one hand, the performance delivery pace of some companies is lower than the most aggressive market expectations; more critically, on the other hand, the market has begun to price in new concerns — easing overseas supply, rising trade risks, and position adjustment after overcrowded A-share AI trading.
Two recent landmark events have pushed this narrative change to a new level.
First, on August 27, 2026, the President of the United States signed an executive order banning the procurement or installation of some foreign-manufactured large power system equipment and related software in the United States. On the same day, A-share transmission and distribution equipment and inverter stocks collectively fell: Siyuan Electric hit the limit-down, Sungrow Power once plunged 14% during the session, and Jinpan Technology dropped by more than 7%.
Second, in September 2026, UBS downgraded the rating of China's electrical equipment industry. UBS pointed out that the sector has fallen by 30% to 50% from its high point within the year, mainly due to the reverse position adjustment of AI trading and the faster-than-expected easing of the global shortage of transformers and gas turbines; it also predicted that exporters will face share and profit margin pressure from 2028 to 2029.
The data at individual stock level is more intuitive. From the beginning of 2025 to the high point in 2026, the maximum increase of Sifang Co., Ltd., Siyuan Electric, Sungrow Power, and Jinpan Technology exceeded 400%, 220%, 160%, and 170% respectively; then they retraced from the high point by around 50%.
The Queue for Hong Kong Listings Remains Fervent
When the market cools down from a hot state, electrical equipment companies have all set their sights on the Hong Kong stock market. Companies including Siyuan Electric and Eagle Energy have successively disclosed prospectuses on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, forming "A+H" dual listings. In fact, after the sharp drop in A-shares, the offering price on the Hong Kong stock market will inevitably be greatly discounted, which is equivalent to diluting the equity of original shareholders at a low level.
However, the pace of companies raising funds in Hong Kong has not slowed down, but is even somewhat eager to outperform each other. The biggest story driving this trend is going global — no matter participating in overseas grid equipment renewal or undertaking data center construction, the reasons for going global seem sufficiently convincing.
Figure: Summary of representative prospectuses of electrical equipment companies applying for Hong Kong stock listing Source: JinDuan Research Institute
The overseas electrical equipment market is huge, with a scale about 4 times that of China's domestic market.
Take the broad-caliber market size given in Eagle Energy's prospectus as an example: the global electrical equipment market size exceeded 8.5 trillion yuan in 2025, and is expected to exceed 12 trillion yuan in 2030, with a CAGR of over 7%. At the same time, electrical equipment under the traditional decentralized distribution architecture is facing the bottlenecks of low efficiency, high redundancy and large space occupation, and the demand for upgrading and iteration is clear.
Figure: Discussion on global electrical equipment in Eagle Energy's prospectus Source: Prospectus
Going global is upgrading from "receiving orders" to "building systems". Overseas certification cycles often last for months to a year, the barriers for customer access are high, and companies also need to cope with localization requirements brought by policy fluctuations. To gain a firm foothold overseas, a complete layout of overseas production capacity, local services, channels and compliance systems is required, all of which require substantial capital expenditure.
The Hong Kong stock market just provides an international capital platform — financing, mergers and acquisitions, employee incentives, and brand endorsement can all be realized in this market.
However, a cold water comes immediately, which is geopolitical restrictions. The U.S. executive order and the EU's restrictive measures are also brewing. Major regions are trying to promote the "sovereignization" of equipment supply chains, and these policy orientations will significantly raise the risk discount of overseas orders on customer access and geopolitical uncertainty.
So the question arises: against the backdrop of sluggish stock prices, do enterprises still have sufficient reasons to queue up for discounted additional issuance in Hong Kong? To answer this question, we need to examine the domestic and overseas markets respectively.
Domestic Market: Stable Fundamental Base, But Limited Imagination Space
China's domestic electrical equipment sector is a large single market, whose core demand comes from the centralized procurement of State Grid Corporation of China and China Southern Power Grid. The advantage is that the two grids have been promoting localization for many years. At present, except for UHV components, the vast majority of electrical equipment has been localized; moreover, the harsh and complex working conditions in China have also put the technical strength of domestic enterprises in the global first echelon.
But in terms of pure industrial logic, the only variable for the prosperity of domestic grid equipment has always been the capital expenditure of the power grid. Therefore, electrical equipment is a typical capital expenditure-driven industry, whose business model is not outstanding.
Entering the "15th Five-Year Plan" period, State Grid has clarified 4 trillion yuan of fixed asset investment, China Southern Power Grid's five-year investment scale is approaching 1 trillion yuan, and the total investment of the two grids is likely to exceed 5 trillion yuan. The mainstream market expectation is that the average annual growth rate of national grid investment from 2026 to 2030 is slightly over 8%, which is still significantly higher than the GDP growth rate — from the total volume perspective, this is still a pretty good industry.
However, while the total volume center rises, the pressure is more reflected in prices. The demand for grid equipment is almost entirely dominated by the two grids, and the volume of State Grid is about 5 times that of China Southern Power Grid; tenders are organized by the unified platform of the two grids, and the customers have extremely strong bargaining power, which can be called the strongest buyer's market in the world.
Historical data has illustrated the problem: low and medium voltage and distribution network products are highly standardized, with fierce homogeneous competition. The average gross profit margin of the sector has long hovered at around 18%, the gross profit margin of cables is just over 10%, and that of transformers is about 20%, all significantly lower than the overseas market.
Since there is limited room to make a difference in the total volume, can enterprises achieve excess returns (alpha) by expanding product categories and increasing market share? In fact, the market structure in China is very difficult to change.
Electrical equipment is widely recognized as a decentralized industry with high research barriers. The horizontal products are extremely scattered, and primary/secondary equipment, AC/DC and different voltage levels cross to form more than 10 sub-segments; most domestic enterprises focus on several sub-segments, with prominent sub-segment/product-oriented characteristics.
The long-term solidified domestic market structure is rooted in the fact that downstream customers will make restrictive institutional arrangements for market share in centralized bidding; at the same time, the high technical and reliability barriers in the primary high-voltage and UHV segments lead to very few new entrants.
One overlooked side effect is that although grid customers have obtained cost-effective equipment supply, the platformization capability of electrical equipment enterprises has been suppressed since the very beginning. Compared with full-industry chain giants such as Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, and Hitachi Energy, domestic enterprises are far behind in scale and system integration capabilities.

AGENCY:
Office of Environmental Management, Department of Energy.
ACTION:
Notice of open meeting.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces an in-person meeting of the Environmental Management Site-Specific Advisory Board (EM SSAB), Portsmouth. The Federal Advisory Committee Act requires that public notice of this meeting be announced in the
Federal Register
.
DATES:
Tuesday, November 17, 2026; 6-8 p.m. EST.
ADDRESSES:
The Ohio State University, Endeavor Center, 1862 Shyville Road, Room 165, Piketon, Ohio 45661.

Greg Simonton, Deputy Designated Federal Officer, Phone: (740) 897-3737 or Email:
greg.simonton@pppo.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Purpose of the Board:
At the request of the Assistant Secretary or Field Managers, the Board may provide community-based advice and recommendations concerning any EM program activities, such as clean-up activities and environmental restoration; waste management and disposition; excess facilities; future land use and long-term stewardship; communications; and budget priorities. The Board also provides an avenue to fulfill public participation requirements outlined in the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERLA), Federal Facility Agreements, Consent Orders, Consent Decrees and Settlement Agreements.
Tentative Agenda:
(agenda topics are subject to change; please contact Greg Simonton for the most current agenda)
Presentation to the Board
Administrative Activities
Public Comments

The meeting is open to the public and public comment can be given orally or in writing. Fifteen minutes are allocated during the meeting for public comment and those wishing to make oral comment will be given a minimum of two minutes to speak. Written comments received at least two working days prior to the meeting will be provided to the members and included in the meeting minutes. Written comments received within two working days after the meeting will be included in the minutes. For additional information on public comment and to submit written
( printed page 65738)
comment, please contact Greg Simonton. The EM SSAB, Portsmouth, welcomes the attendance of the public at its meetings and will make every effort to accommodate persons with physical disabilities or special needs. The Designated Federal Officer is empowered to conduct the meeting in a fashion that will facilitate the orderly conduct of business. Questioning of board members or presenters by the public is not permitted.

AGENCY:
Food and Drug Administration, HHS.
                    SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration's (FDA or Agency) Center for Drug Evaluation and Research and Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research are announcing support for Forward Compatibility for Electronic Common Technical Document (eCTD) Version 4.0 (v4.0)-based electronic submissions.
                    DATES:
FDA support for Forward Compatibility for eCTD v4.0 electronic submissions begins October 16, 2026. Submit either electronic or written comments at any time.
                    ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments as follows:
Electronic Submissions
Submit electronic comments in the following way:
- Federal eRulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov.
                     Follow the instructions for submitting comments. Comments submitted electronically, including attachments, to 
                    https://www.regulations.gov
                     will be posted to the docket unchanged. Because your comment will be made public, you are solely responsible for ensuring that your comment does not include any confidential information that you or a third party may not wish to be posted, such as medical information, your or anyone else's Social Security number, or confidential business information, such as a manufacturing process. Please note that if you include your name, contact information, or other information that identifies you in the body of your comments, that information will be posted on 
                    https://www.regulations.gov.
- If you want to submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made available to the public, submit the comment as a written/paper submission and in the manner detailed (see “Written/Paper Submissions” and “Instructions”).
Written/Paper Submissions
Submit written/paper submissions as follows:
- Mail/Hand Delivery/Courier (for written/paper submissions):
                     Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852.
                
- For written/paper comments submitted to the Dockets Management Staff, FDA will post your comment, as well as any attachments, except for information submitted, marked and identified, as confidential, if submitted as detailed in “Instruction.”
                    Instructions:
                     All submissions received must include the Docket No. FDA-2018-D-1216 for “Electronic Common Technical Document; Data Standards; Center for Drug Evaluation and Research and Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research Supporting Electronic Common Technical Document Version 4.0.” Received comments will be placed in the docket and, except for those submitted as “Confidential Submissions,” publicly viewable at 
                    https://www.regulations.gov
                     or at the Dockets Management Staff between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, 240-402-7500.
                
- Confidential Submissions—To submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made publicly available, submit your comments only as a written/paper submission. You should submit two copies total. One copy will include the information you claim to be confidential with a heading or cover note that states “THIS DOCUMENT CONTAINS CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION.” The Agency will review this copy, including the claimed confidential information, in its consideration of comments. The second copy, which will have the claimed confidential information redacted/blacked out, will be available for public viewing and posted onhttps://www.regulations.gov.
                     Submit both copies to the Dockets Management Staff. If you do not wish your name and contact information to be made publicly available, you can provide this information on the cover sheet and not in the body of your comments and you must identify this information as “confidential.” Any information marked as “confidential” will not be disclosed except in accordance with 21 CFR 10.20 and other applicable disclosure law. For more information about FDA's posting of comments to public dockets, see 80 FR 56469, September 18, 2015, or access the information at: 
                    https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2015-09-18/pdf/2015-23389.pdf.
                    Docket:
                     For access to the docket to read background documents or the electronic and written/paper comments received, go to 
                    https://www.regulations.gov
                     and insert the docket number, found in brackets in the heading of this document, into the “Search” box and follow the prompts and/or go to the Dockets Management Staff, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852, 240-402-7500.

The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) will prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) that will discuss the environmental impacts of the Texas Gateway Project involving construction and operation of facilities by Gulf South Pipeline Company, LLC (Gulf South) in Panola, Shelby, San Augustine, Sabine, Jasper, Newton, and San Jacinto counties, Texas and Beauregard Parish, Louisiana. The Commission will use this EIS in its decision-making process to determine whether the project is in the public convenience and necessity.
As part of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process, the Commission takes into account concerns the public may have about proposals and the environmental impacts that could result from its action whenever it considers the issuance of a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. This gathering of public input is referred to as “scoping.” The main goal of the scoping process is to focus the analysis in the environmental document on the important environmental issues. On August 25, 2026, the Commission issued a
Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement for the Proposed Texas Gateway Project, Request for Comments on Environmental Issues, and Schedule for Environmental Review
(NOI). Through the NOI, the Commission initiated an initial public scoping period and requested comments on the scope of environmental issues to be addressed in the EIS. With this current Notice, the Commission is announcing an additional scoping period, which will also allow interested stakeholders an opportunity to participate in in-person scoping sessions. Comments received during the previous and current scoping periods will be considered in the Commission staff's environmental review and in the development of the EIS. Additional information about the Commission's NEPA process is described below in the
NEPA Process and Environmental Document
section of this notice.
By this notice, the Commission requests public comments on the scope of issues to address in the EIS. To ensure that your comments are timely and properly recorded, please submit your comments so that the Commission receives them in Washington, DC on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 12, 2026. Comments may be submitted in written or oral form. Further details on how to submit comments are provided in the
Public Participation
section of this notice.
Your comments should focus on the potential environmental effects, reasonable alternatives, and measures to avoid or lessen environmental impacts. Your input will help the Commission staff determine what issues they need to evaluate in the EIS. Commission staff will consider all written or oral comments during the preparation of the EIS.
If you submitted comments on this project to the Commission before the opening of this docket on June 26, 2026, you will need to file those comments in Docket No. CP26-547-000 to ensure they are considered as part of this proceeding.
This notice is being sent to the Commission's current environmental mailing list for this project. State and local government representatives should notify their constituents of this proposed project and encourage them to comment on their areas of concern.
If you are a landowner receiving this notice, a pipeline company representative may contact you about the acquisition of an easement to construct, operate, and maintain the proposed facilities. The company would seek to negotiate a mutually acceptable easement agreement. You are not required to enter into an agreement. However, if the Commission approves the project, the Natural Gas Act conveys the right of eminent domain to the company. Therefore, if you and the company do not reach an easement agreement, the pipeline company could initiate condemnation proceedings in court. In such instances, compensation would be determined by a judge in accordance with state law. The Commission does not subsequently grant, exercise, or oversee the exercise of that eminent domain authority. The courts have exclusive authority to handle eminent domain cases; the Commission has no jurisdiction over these matters.
Gulf South provided landowners with a fact sheet prepared by the FERC entitled “An Interstate Natural Gas Facility On My Land? What Do I Need To Know?” which addresses typically asked questions, including the use of eminent domain and how to participate in the Commission's proceedings. This
( printed page 65743)
fact sheet along with other landowner topics of interest are available for viewing on the FERC website (
www.ferc.gov) under the Natural Gas, Landowner Topics link.
Public Participation
There are four methods you can use to submit your comments to the Commission. Please carefully follow these instructions so that your comments are properly recorded. The Commission encourages electronic filing of comments and has staff available to assist you at (866) 208-3676 or
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov.
(1) You can file your comments electronically using the eComment feature, which is located on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. Using eComment is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments on a project;
(2) You can file your comments electronically by using the eFiling feature, which is located on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” You will be asked to select the type of filing you are making; a comment on a particular project is considered a “Comment on a Filing”;
(3) You can file a paper copy of your comments by mailing them to the Commission. Be sure to reference the project docket number (CP26-547-000) on your letter. Submissions sent via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, MD 20852; or

The post I guest host the NYT podcast and interview Dwarkesh appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Excerpt:

Cowen: Unreleased models — why are they important?
Patel: As in the ones that are internal to the companies?
Cowen: Well, many companies have unreleased models. Maybe it would cost too much to release them or they’re not safe yet, but the public doesn’t see them.
Patel: Yeah.
Cowen: You’re an insider. Whether or not you see them, you hear about them; you know something about them. How should we think about unreleased models, and how does that change our picture of what’s going on?
Patel: I think there’s a very frustrating element to the current situation right now, where people inside the A.I. labs claim to have evidence that makes them more worried, and they are not allowed to talk about it. This makes it a very difficult situation on the outside to evaluate how worried we should be.
For example, maybe two days ago, I was talking to somebody at Anthropic, and they were like: Look, I expect A.I.s to beat humans at A.I. research within nine months.
And I’m like: Why do you believe that?
They’re like: It’s not just vibes, but I have information on the inside.




I’m like: What is it? Is it a new model? Is it some evaluation you ran?
He’s like: I can’t talk about it.
I think it’s a terrible state of affairs. If they really believe this, if they think that we’re in a situation where we’re less than a year away from automating A.I. research and radically speeding it up, they should make this evidence public.
I especially worry about the following scenario, whereas A.I.s get better and better at making A.I. progress faster and automating it, they will be inclined not to keep releasing models that are even close to their smartest models externally, because then if they release those externally, it would help others make smart models.
And it’s just kind of a schlep to release models externally. You need all these safeguards and everything.
Cowen: So the gap between what they know and what we know would get bigger and bigger under that scenario. We’d end up more in the dark, more surprised when things happen. It would be harder for regulators, policymakers, members of Congress, everyone.

Kudos to Dwarkesh for taking the other side of the microphone.  Do also see our discussion of AI psychosis, among other topics.

AGENCY:
Office of Administration, Executive Office of the President.
ACTION:
Notice of availability; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
Consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, as amended (NHPA), this Notice announces the availability and opportunity for public review and comment of a draft Environmental Assessment (EA), which examines the potential impacts of a proposal by the Office of Administration (OA), Executive Office of the President (EOP), to improve the granite façade of the Dwight D. Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB). Pursuant to this notice, OA is also seeking public comment on the potential of the proposed improvements to cause adverse effects on historic properties. Finally, this notice provides information on how individuals and organizations may request to become consulting parties.
DATES:
This notice initiates a public comment period for the Draft EA. OA requests that the public submit comments concerning the scope of the analysis, potential alternatives, and identification of relevant information and studies by November 16, 2026. To afford OA the opportunity to consider comments, please ensure any comments are received prior to the close of the 30-day comment period.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, identified by docket number OA-2026-0001, by any of the following methods:
Email:FedRegComments@oa.eop.gov. Include docket number OA-2026-0001 in the subject line of the message.
Instructions:
All submissions received outside of
Regulations.gov
must include the name “Office of Administration” and the docket number for this notice of availability. OA makes all comments, including the names, addresses, and other personally identifiable information included in the comment, available for public review online. Individuals can request that OA withhold their names, addresses, or other personally identifiable information included in their comment from the public record; however, OA cannot guarantee that it will be able to do so.
All submissions from organizations or businesses and from individuals identifying themselves as representatives or officials of organizations or businesses will be made available for public inspection in their entirety.
Office of Administration, Heather Martin, Deputy Director and Chief Financial Officer, (202) 456-4646,
FedRegNotices@oa.eop.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Introduction
The Draft EA evaluates the potential environmental impacts of a proposal by OA to make improvements to the granite façade of the EEOB and bring it into visual alignment with the neighboring White House. Section 590 of Public Law 100-461 authorizes the OA Director to accept gifts, property, and voluntary services to support renovation and rehabilitation of the EEOB, and establishes a United States Treasury Fund for those purposes. OA is not a Federal agency and is therefore is not required to comply with either NEPA or the NHPA. Moreover, given the EEOB's location on White House grounds, it is exempt from the requirements of the NHPA under Section 107. Nonetheless, OA is voluntarily following the NEPA and NHPA procedures for this Project because those procedures provide a generally well-understood framework for considering potential effects and receiving input from agencies, the public, and interested parties.
Purpose of and Need for the Proposed Action
The subject of the Project, the EEOB, is located to the west of the White House at 17th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW. The Project is proposed to rehabilitate and improve the granite façade of the EEOB to restore and beautify its physical appearance, consistent with Executive Order 14344, Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again. At present, several areas of the EEOB's façade are deteriorating, including through granular disintegration, delamination, incipient spalling, cracking, and chipping, as well as gypsum salt accumulation, efflorescence, stains from exposure to contaminants, and biological growth. This deterioration has worsened over time and diminished the EEOB's appearance and stature. Further, the gray façade of the EEOB, combined with its size and massing, conveys a dark, drab, and uninspiring presence that detracts from the aesthetic presentation of the much smaller White House directly adjacent to it. In carrying out proposed exterior improvements, OA proposes to address existing areas of degradation, engage in various masonry preservation measures, and coat the façade with white, mineral silicate paint. The proposed action would not only address areas of disrepair on the EEOB's façade, but would also visually align the EEOB with the White House, of which it is a functional extension.
Alternatives Under Consideration
The EA will consider three Action Alternatives (
i.e.,
the Exterior Painting Alternative, the Partial Painting Alternative, and the Cleaning and Lighting Alternative) and the No Action Alternative. Under the Exterior Painting Alternative (the “Preferred Alternative”), the EEOB's whole granite façade (excluding interior courtyards) would be painted with a white, mineral silicate paint. Prior to painting, the granite facade would be prepared for
( printed page 65715)
painting, which would include a conservation-based cleaning regimen and stone repair and preservation measures implemented in accordance with the Secretary of Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties. articles.title: Emissions Value Request Process; Notice of Availability
articles.summary: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) hereby provides notice of availability of the Emissions Value Request Process in support of the U.S. Department of the Treasury's (Treasury) and Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) administration of the section 45Z Credit for Clean Fuel Production.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, U.S. Department of Energy.
                    ACTION:
Notice of availability.
                    SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) hereby provides notice of availability of the Emissions Value Request Process in support of the U.S. Department of the Treasury's (Treasury) and Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) administration of the section 45Z Credit for Clean Fuel Production.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 
The Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit (Internal Revenue Code Section 45Z) was established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-169), and amended by the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21). The amount of the tax credit is determined, in part, by the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of the transportation fuel.
Transportation fuel producers seeking to claim the tax credit must obtain the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of their transportation fuel using the applicable emissions rate table published for section 45Z, or by petitioning the Secretary of Treasury for a provisional emissions rate (PER) if the fuel's type, primary feedstock, or pathway is not included in the applicable emissions rate table. The Treasury and IRS issued notice 2025-10 (January 2025), section 45Z clean fuel production credit; request for public comments, which provided that an applicant seeking a PER must follow the latest procedures for obtaining a PER as published by the Secretary Treasury in the section 45Z regulations and in the Internal Revenue Bulletin, including the process for obtaining an emissions value from DOE that is used by the applicant to request a PER determination. On July 24, 2025, DOE published a notice of intent and request for comment regarding an Emissions Value Request process. 90 FR 34855. On February 4, 2026, the Treasury and IRS published a notice of proposed rulemaking, which proposed the procedures that a taxpayer must follow to request a PER determination. 91 FR 5160, 5173.
DOE has considered the comments received regarding the Emissions Value Request Process, and is now announcing the opening of the 45Z Emissions Value Request Process.
Signing Authority
                    This document of the Department of Energy was signed on October 13, 2026, by Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary (EERE) for Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, pursuant to delegated authority from the Secretary of Energy. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DOE. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DOE Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of the Department of Energy. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the 
                    Federal Register
                    .
                
                    Signed in Washington, DC, on October 14, 2026.
Treena V. Garrett,
Federal Register Liaison Officer, U.S. Department of Energy.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action revokes Very High Frequency (VHF) Omnidirectional Range (VOR) Federal Airway V-320 in Alaska due to navigational signal limits causing portions of this route to be unusable. There are two routes with the identifier V-320, one located in the state of Alaska, and one located in the state of Michigan. This action only revokes the V-320 located in Alaska. FAA is also establishing United States Area Navigation (RNAV) Route T-550 near Anchorage, AK.
DATES:

Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it would amend the airway structure as necessary to preserve the safe and efficient flow of air traffic within the National Airspace System.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-1993 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 8796; February 24, 2026), proposing to revoke V-320 and to establish RNAV Route T-550 in the state of Alaska. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. No comments were received.
Incorporation by Reference
RNAV Routes are published in paragraph 6011 and VOR Federal Airways are in paragraph 6010(b) of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action amends 14 CFR part 71 by revoking V-320 and establishing RNAV Route T-550 in the state of Alaska.
V-320:
Prior to this final rule, V-320 extended between the McGrath, AK, VOR/Tactical Air Navigation (VORTAC) and the Johnstone Point, AK, VHF/Distance Measuring Equipment (VOR/DME). Due to navigational signal limits causing portions of this route to be unusable, the FAA is revoking V-320 in its entirety.
T-550:
The FAA is establishing T-550 as a new route between the FRIDA, AK, Fix and the Anchorage, AK, VOR/DME to provide coverage for segments of V-320 that do not overlay existing airways.

The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary special local regulation (SLR) for certain navigable waters of Lake Havasu. This action is necessary to provide for the safety of life on these navigable waters near Lake Havasu City, AZ during the Pineapple Races event beginning at 3 p.m. on October 20, 2026, and ending the evening of October 20, 2026, at 8 p.m. This regulation prohibits persons and vessels from entering the regulated area unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port San Diego or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 3 p.m. through 8 p.m. on October 20, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact Lieutenant Skye Eastman, Sector San Diego Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 619-454-9027, or email
MarineEventsSD@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
SLR Special Local Regulation
( printed page 65686)
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received a request under 33 CFR 100.15 from the Lake Havasu Chamber of Commerce for a Marine Event Permit to host canoe races. The event will be held from 3 p.m. to 8 p.m. on October 20, 2026, in Lake Havasu City, AZ. The canoe races will include approximately 175 participants.
The Captain of the Port San Diego (COTP) is issuing this Special Local Regulation (SLR) under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70041. The COTP has determined that potential hazards associated with the Pineapple Races include the obstruction of the navigable channel due to the event's location and duration, as well as the high number of participants and canoes involved. The event will require partial closure of the Bridgewater Channel to vessel traffic in both directions during race operations, with designated cross times in between races to allow limited vessel passage. These conditions present increased risks of collision, congestion, and interference with the normal flow of marine traffic. The purpose of this rulemaking is to ensure the safety of event participants, non-participating mariners, and transiting vessels before, during, and after the scheduled event.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. The Coast Guard was not notified of this event with sufficient time to solicit comments before this SLR must be established on October 20, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reasons, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a temporary SLR from 3 p.m. until 8 p.m. on October 20, 2026. The special local regulation will cover all navigable waters within 100 yards of the canoe races. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the regulated area without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, 5 U.S.C. 601-612, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-121), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under Executive Order 13132, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (2 U.S.C. 1531-1538), the Coast Guard certifies that this rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321et seq.), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions

articles.title: India has more Restrictive Labor Law than Germany
articles.summary:
In Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State, Shruti Rajagopalan and I discuss how India has essentially all of the laws of a developed country but at much lower state capacity–this mismatch creates what we call premature imitation, with a host of negative consequences. What is even more amazing, however, is when a country like India […]
The post India has more Restrictive Labor Law than Germany appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
In Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State, Shruti Rajagopalan and I discuss how India has essentially all of the laws of a developed country but at much lower state capacity–this mismatch creates what we call premature imitation, with a host of negative consequences. What is even more amazing, however, is when a country like India regulates beyond most developed countries. Anand, Chandra, and Pradeep provide a case in point at Prosperity Insights–India regulates labor hours more than Germany.
Germany and India share an 8 hour standard working day but India requires any overtime to be paid at twice the regular rate–most developed countries are at 1.5 and a few have no statutory cap at all. In fact, Germany has no statutory overtime rate–it can vary depending on bargaining. Germany is also more flexible than India on the number of overtime hours. India has a cap of 144 overtime hours a quarter. Technically, Germany doesn’t regulate overtime hours but it does cap total hours at 10 a day and 48 a week on average. The average is crucial. In Germany overtime hours can be moved between weeks within a 6 month period while India regulates each week. In other words, long weeks in Germany are legal as long as short weeks offset them before the period ends–while in India each week has a cap. The weekly cap and the double overtime pay make it very costly and difficult to meet rush or large seasonal orders.
Consider a hypothetical 500-worker electronics factory, working a single shift, in each of the 16 countries studied. Ahead of a September iPhone launch, each factory receives an order for 10,000 devices to be completed in three months.
Say the factories are identical in productivity, wages and technology; only the rules on working hours differ. How fast and at what labour cost would the Indian factory deliver compared to elsewhere?
The results are stark.
The factory in India cannot match the pace of its global peers. It takes 13.7 weeks to complete the 10,000-iPhone order, 23% longer than the fastest factory…The Indian factory falls behind because it cannot keep the same pace throughout the production cycle. Without the option to rearrange regular hours, the only way to go faster is overtime…The Indian factory cannot compete on cost either. To complete the iPhone order, it pays for 49.3 labour-hours per unit, at least 18% more than factories at the cost frontier. India’s unit cost is high because 144 of the 800 production hours per worker are paid as overtime at 2x the regular wage, pushing paid labour to 985 hours for 800 hours of output.
…The combination of slow delivery and high cost makes India an unattractive manufacturing destination.
Amazingly, on an equal-wage basis producing iPhones in Germany is actually cheaper and faster than in India! Of course, wages are not equal but neither is productivity–the key point is that the chart isolates the cost of India’s regulatory inflexibility.
Returning to premature imitation, it won’t surprise you that many firms and workers in India evade the overtime rules and come to their own understandings but this applies mostly to small Indian firms and not the Foxconns and big international firms that India wants to attract but which must obey the laws as written.
Hat tip: Paul Novosad.

articles.title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account
articles.summary: Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offenderUS lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.
It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.
A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.
If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.
The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.
Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.
Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.
The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.
Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.
That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.
After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.
In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.
Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.
The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.
“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.
Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”
Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

articles.full_text:
I first saw Ingmar Bergman’s Persona, his stone-cold classic of 1965, as a teenager, and God knows how many times I have seen it since. It has the greatest opening sequence in cinema: a percussive, rapid-fire montage that can never be wholly accommodated or understood. The film’s story is, however, a simple one (even if its Jungian resonances are deep and complex). A celebrated actress, Elisabeth Vogler (one of Liv Ullmann’s defining roles), is struck dumb, having dried up in the middle of a performance of Electra. Three months later, still speechless, she is granted a nurse, Alma (Bibi Andersson), who, fearing silence, cannot stop talking to and at her patient. Elisabeth becomes the audience, Alma the performer, and the two personalities intertwine against a biblical monochrome landscape of sand, rock and water. More than 60 years on, it remains inexhaustible, never to be entirely absorbed, intimate, stark and utterly compelling.
Here is more from Paul Lay.

articles.full_text: Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for allThe trouble with economists, Isabella Weber believes, is they do not behave like dentists. They obsess over ideological purity and are inflexible when searching for solutions, regardless of society’s symptoms. Dentists have no such pretensions – patients have little patience for dogma when in insufferable pain.John Maynard Keynes, Weber clarifies in the canteen of the Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin (Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study), was the first to draw this dental comparison – and she is running with it. As she sees it, the symptoms could not be more severe. “The status quo for the majority is entirely unbearable,” while extreme inequality and corporate concentration has reached levels “simply incompatible with democracy” worldwide. This is exacerbated by a climate crisis that “generates massive windfall profits” for big business as the “ecological foundations of our lives disintegrate”. All the while the far right is making hay. Continue reading...

AGENCY:
Office of Adjudication, Recruitment, and Management, Justice Management Division, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
60-Day notice.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Attorney Recruitment and Management (OARM), Justice Management Division (JMD), Department of Justice (DOJ), will be submitting the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995.
DATES:
Comments are encouraged and will be accepted for 60 days until December 15, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have additional comments especially on the estimated public burden or associated response time, suggestions, or need a copy of the proposed information collection instrument with instructions or additional information, please contact Michael E. Stamp, Office of Adjudication, Recruitment, and Management, 450 5th St. NW, Suite 10200, (202) 514-3905.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Written comments and suggestions from the public and affected agencies concerning the proposed collection of information are encouraged. Your comments should address one or more of the following four points:
—Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the (component), including whether the information will have practical utility;
—Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
—Evaluate whether and if so how the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected can be enhanced; and
—Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses.
